overview: Physics Sim is a browser-based MuJoCo rigid-body physics simulator. Scenes are defined as a tree of SceneNode bodies, each with primitive geoms and joints. The simulator compiles scenes to MJCF XML and runs MuJoCo WASM in the browser. Coordinate system: X=right, Y=forward/depth, Z=up. Ground plane at Z=0.
workflow: 1. Call physics_get_schema to understand available geom/joint types and fields.
2. Use physics_build_scene (easy, auto-fills defaults) or physics_update_scene (full control).
3. For an organic or particular shape (a face, an animal, a worn tool) use physics_create_sculpt and physics_sculpt rather than primitives or OpenSCAD. See schema.sculpting.
4. For a crisp dimensioned part (a bracket, a housing, a mount) use physics_create_lattice and physics_lattice_extrude: exact coordinates on a grid. See schema.lattice.

5. Use physics_run_headless to simulate N ticks and verify behaviour programmatically: check final positions, velocities, or trajectory shape against expected values. Do this before relying on visual inspection.
6. Call physics_play to show the simulation to the user once you have confirmed it behaves correctly via headless run.

7. Call physics_set_note_cards to put a card on the scene describing what was built: its title, its dimensions, and the physics it demonstrates. A scene without one is not finished; see that tool's description for the shape of a good card.
8. Use physics_set_environment to adjust gravity, wind, floor friction, and fluid density.
gotchas: HOLLOW SHAPES NOW COLLIDE AS HOLLOW SHAPES, so do not build proxy walls. MuJoCo itself collides a mesh as its CONVEX HULL, which fills in any cavity — a cup, bowl, open-top box, funnel or housing would be solid and a ball dropped in would rest on an invisible lid at the rim. The app now measures each body's SOLIDITY (true volume over hull volume) and breaks anything below ~0.92 into convex pieces automatically, for every kind of mesh body: imported STL, sculpt, lattice, relief, SCAD, boolean. Model the container as a container. physics_get_scene_summary reports `collidesAs` and `solidity` per body, and `cavityFilled` when a hollow body is still colliding as its hull. Override with `collision`: 'hull' forces the old filled-in behaviour, 'decompose' forces the split. ONE CONSEQUENCE: a decomposed hollow body is weighed by its true volume rather than its hull's — often a third as much — so set `mass` or `collisionMass` if you wanted the heavier figure.

A body that looks TRANSPARENT or see-through is rarely a transparency setting. Check its rgba alpha (below 1 draws translucent); if that is 1, the usual cause is inside-out face winding, because mesh geoms are drawn single-sided: the near surface is culled and you are looking at the inside of the far wall through the gap where it should be. Call physics_get_scene_summary and read `windingInverted` on the geom before you touch colours or materials.

DO NOT add a body with a plane geom as a floor. MuJoCo provides a built-in ground plane at Z=0 automatically. Adding a plane body causes a silent compile error: the scene loads but physics_play returns ok:true while isPlaying stays false. Omit the floor body entirely.

After calling physics_play, immediately call physics_get_state and check that isPlaying is true. If it is still false, the scene failed to compile (likely a bad geom, duplicate name, or plane body conflict). Fix the scene and try again.
Script functions require the 'api.' prefix. Writing getTime() instead of api.getTime() throws ReferenceError and silently breaks the script. All api calls must be api.functionName(...).
To give a body an initial velocity, use a script with a first-tick guard: if (api.getTime() === 0) { api.setVelocity([...], 'bodyName'); }. Using === 0 fires exactly on the first tick.

The script field on a SceneNode is a single string: 'script': '...'. It is NOT an array. Passing scripts:[{code:'...'}] or scripts:['...'] will silently be ignored and the script will never run. Always use the singular 'script' key with a flat string value.

Bodies that should NOT collide with each other (e.g. windmill blades, rotor hub, nacelle) MUST have contype:0 AND conaffinity:0 on ALL their geoms. Without this, sibling bodies that overlap near a shared parent origin generate huge contact-constraint forces that oscillate and prevent scripted torques from accumulating. Even a few millimetres of geom overlap near the hub causes ±1 rad/s oscillation that prevents spin-up.

api.getOrientation() returns the 9-element row-major rotation matrix of the body the script is attached to (xmat). Column 0 = [R[0], R[3], R[6]] is the body's local X-axis in world space. For a rotor with hinge axis=[1,0,0], project wind onto this axis to get the effective wind speed: Vw = windX*R[0] + windY*R[3].

physics_update_scene's sceneGraph parameter is a bare array of SceneNode objects (matching physics_build_scene's bodies convention), NOT { nodes: [...] }. Passing the wrapped object form is tolerated but the array form is canonical.

physics_build_scene and physics_update_scene wait for any scad bodies to finish compiling and for a final MJCF recompile before responding, and report the real result as { ok, error?, nodeCount }. There is no need to poll physics_get_state afterward. The call can take several seconds for scenes with multiple scad bodies (each compiles sequentially).

physics_get_state.lastCompileError holds the most recent MJCF/MuJoCo compile error message (or null on success). Check this after loading a scene to see the real underlying failure reason instead of just a generic ok:false.

OpenSCAD designs in this simulator must be scaled to meters (scale([0.001, 0.001, 0.001]) { ... }) at the top-level. Leaving them in default millimeters causes meshes to render 1000x too large, breaking camera zoom bounding boxes and physics stability.

To visually verify layout, spacing, or alignment of a scene, use the physics_get_screenshot tool directly rather than launching a Puppeteer or browser instance. Spawning browser instances is slow, resource-heavy, and redundant when the direct viewport screenshot tool is available.

The browser-based WASM compiler used in the physics app (openscad-wasm) does not have system font files mounted in its virtual filesystem. Calling text() in OpenSCAD fails silently (compiles to empty geometry without errors). To draw text labels on a SCAD mesh, construct the letters manually using line segments (e.g. hull() of circles or cylinders in 2D or 3D) to guarantee cross-platform compilation.

When performing CSG difference operations in OpenSCAD (such as cutting slots, grooves, or recesses), ensure the subtracted geometries extend slightly past the outer boundaries of the main body. Perfectly coplanar faces at the cutting limits can cause degenerate triangles or rendering artifacts (like flickering or jagged ridges) in the WebGL renderer.
To load a user preset, use the 'user:presetName' format (e.g. 'user:mukada') in the physics_load_preset parameter. The bridge handles this automatically by pulling from localStorage.

If a dynamic mesh's visual representation is misaligned or hovering compared to its collision behavior, verify the renderVertices: they should be a direct swap: (x, -z, y) of the Y-up collision vertices without subtracting the centroid (since MuJoCo handles centroid offset internally).

Never bypass the MCP API surface by creating raw browser agents or Puppeteer connections to query state or localStorage, and do not modify source code files simply to add telemetry/debug commands. Use the existing MCP endpoints to query state (e.g. physics_get_state) and apply updates (e.g. physics_update_scene).

Ensure geom size arrays match the required element count for each primitive: 'capsule' requires 2 elements [radius, half_length] (or use fromto), 'cylinder' requires 2 elements [radius, half_height], 'box' requires 3 elements [hx, hy, hz], and 'sphere' requires 1 element [radius]. A 1-element capsule with no fromto does NOT error and does NOT disappear: the MJCF writer falls back to half_length = radius, so the intended rod/spoke/arm silently becomes a tiny stub pill at the geom's pos. Since such geoms usually also default to pos:[0,0,0], several of them (e.g. the five arms of a star) stack into ONE small blob at the body origin. A single unexplained capsule at the centre of a body is almost always this, not a renderer or simulator fault. Inspect the geoms with physics_get_object and look for 1-element capsule sizes.

Visual geoms and bodies (such as capsule rods, hub rings, bearings, and axle pins) mounted near shared joint pivot origins MUST have contype:0 AND conaffinity:0 set on their geoms. Without contype:0/conaffinity:0, overlapping geoms near the pivot origin generate strong contact interpenetration forces that lock the joint and cause high-frequency wobbling in place instead of smooth swinging.
When constructing or updating hinge joints, always explicitly specify the rotation axis (e.g. axis:[0,1,0]). Omitting axis causes MuJoCo to default to [0,0,1], breaking planar hinge motion.

When mutating or generating scene nodes, preserve existing capsule span attributes (fromto or 2-element size), collision flags (contype:0/conaffinity:0), and joint axes so rods and pivots do not disappear or jam after scene updates.

When generating parametric OpenSCAD scripts (such as sine waves, splines, or ribbons), ALWAYS declare design parameters (e.g. wave_length = 50; // [10:5:200], thickness = 2.0; // [0.5:0.5:10]) on separate lines at the VERY TOP of the SCAD code, outside any scale(), module, or function blocks. Include Customizer range annotations // [min:step:max] so the app can automatically parse them into interactive UI sliders.
Copilot response parsing rule: diagnostic 'questions' arrays (containing question/options keys) must NEVER be treated as scene 'nodes'. Scene nodes require valid body/geom/scad structure.

A body with a 'scad' script compiles to exactly ONE mesh geom that IS the entire part. The SCAD source is the single source of truth for that body's shape. When converting a primitive-built body to SCAD, or rewriting its SCAD, you MUST also replace its geoms array with just that one mesh geom. Leftover primitives from the previous version are not ignored: they still render and still collide on top of the mesh, and because they are typically unpositioned (pos:[0,0,0], no fromto) they pile up at the body's centre as stray blobs and discs that look like simulator artefacts. Note that physics_update_object with a 'scad' payload only refills the existing mesh geom; it does NOT prune sibling primitives, so send an explicit geoms array to remove them. A dynamic mesh already collides via its convex hull, so do not keep primitives around 'for collision' unless you want a proxy. In that case position it explicitly and set contype:0/conaffinity:0 on whichever geom must not collide.

Do not use rgba alpha to hide a helper/bounds geom. Alpha below 1 draws a geom translucent, and 0 makes it invisible, but either way it still collides and still has mass: an invisible bounds box is a wall nothing can pass through. If a geom should not be there, delete it.

THE VIEWPORT IS NOT A VALIDATOR. A scene that looks right can still be unusable: open edges, inverted winding, zero-area triangles and shells that merely touch instead of overlapping are all invisible on screen and all break an export. physics_get_lattice and physics_get_sculpt report `watertight` on every reply for exactly this reason — read it. A raw mesh geom you built yourself has no such guard, so check it before you rely on it, and prefer physics_create_lattice or physics_create_sculpt when the thing is going to be made rather than only looked at.

A screenshot is evidence about APPEARANCE and nothing else. It cannot show you that a mesh is closed, that a wall is the thickness you asked for, that two parts are joined rather than overlapping, or that a dimension is what you intended. Use physics_measure for distances, the `watertight` flag for solidity, and the export tools' own warnings for whether a part can actually be made.

coordinateSystem.mujocoWorldSpace: X=right (+X right, -X left), Y=forward into screen (+Y away, -Y toward viewer), Z=up (+Z height). Ground plane at Z=0. Gravity default: Z=-9.81.
coordinateSystem.geomPos: pos field on geoms is a local offset from the body origin in MuJoCo Z-up space.
coordinateSystem.bodyPos: pos field on bodies is relative to parent body (or world origin for root bodies).
coordinateSystem.meshVertices: EXCEPTION: mesh geom vertices are in Three.js Y-up world space (X=right, Y=up, Z=toward camera). See mesh section.
coordinateSystem.cameraOrientation: CAMERA Y-AXIS RULE: In MuJoCo world space, -Y is in front of the object toward the viewer, and +Y is behind the object. To frame a front-on view of an object at target [0, 0, z], set position to a NEGATIVE Y coordinate (e.g. position: [0, -2.5, z], target: [0, 0, z]). Passing a positive Y coordinate (e.g. [0, 2.5, z]) places the camera behind the object looking into empty space.
coordinateSystem.defaultCamera: physics_get_screenshot always renders whatever the viewport camera currently shows. Use physics_set_camera(position, target), both MuJoCo world-space [x,y,z], to point the camera at a specific body/face before screenshotting. To frame a front-on view of an object at [x,y,z], place position at a negative Y offset relative to target (e.g. position:[0, y-2.5, z], target:[x, y, z]). The default 'perspective' preset is a diagonal 3/4 pose. physics_get_camera returns the camera's live pose.

tools.list_sessions:
List the browser tabs connected to each app, and say which one commands are going to.

Several tabs of the same app can be open at once. Without this the hub could only shout at all of them and keep whichever answered first, which makes the app look haunted: a body created by one call is missing from the next, a preset saved over a good one comes back empty, a screenshot shows a scene from twenty minutes ago. Each tab now has an id and a label, and every command goes to exactly one of them.

The most recently connected tab is selected by default, so with one tab open there is nothing to do. With several, call this and then use_session.
tools.physics_add_object:
Add ONE body to the scene, leaving everything already in it alone. `body` is a single body descriptor, exactly the shape of one element of physics_build_scene's `bodies` array, and the same defaults are filled in.

Use this instead of reading the scene back and posting it again through physics_update_scene. On a scene holding a sculpt or a boolean that round trip is megabytes each way, and it overwrites anything another client changed in between. physics_delete_object is the other half of the pair.

An id that is already taken is given a numeric suffix rather than refused, and the reply says what the body was actually called. The reply also carries the real MJCF compile result, so a body that failed to build says so rather than reporting ok and leaving you to find out.
tools.physics_build_scene: Build and load a scene from simplified body descriptors. Auto-fills safe defaults. Easier than physics_update_scene. Waits for any scad bodies to finish compiling and for MJCF to settle before responding. The response is { ok, error?, nodeCount }, so check `ok`/`error` directly rather than polling physics_get_state. Can take several seconds for scenes with multiple scad bodies. After the scene lands, write its note card with physics_set_note_cards; nothing else does. The default card says "Interactive 3D rigid-body physics scene". Replace it as part of building the scene.
tools.physics_carve_scene:
Machine the scene that is loaded. Needs the machine armed. This is the one that cuts.

A solid is machined from more than one SIDE, and the sides are separate programs with the part re-fixtured in between — so this runs ONE side and says which. `side` picks it; the default is the first. Do not treat a carve as a single button press: tell the user the part has to be turned over and the next side run separately, and that Z must be re-zeroed after it is.

`toolDiaMm` (default 3), `sides`, `stockThicknessMm` and `material` shape the program. It refuses if more than 5% of the part cannot be reached by the chosen tool — that comes out as an unmachined lump and the operator finds out three hours in; use a smaller tool, cut from more sides, or pass `acceptUnreachable: true` if that is understood and wanted.

Over a Tekno Box the device runs the program itself and the carve survives the laptop being shut. Over USB this browser is the streamer and the job lives as long as the tab. Poll physics_machine_status for progress — and note that progress is reported as an elapsed clock against an estimate, not as a line count, because a rapid across the stock and a raster pass are both one line and take wildly different times.
tools.physics_check_collisions: Check for initial axis-aligned bounding box overlaps/interpenetrations between scene bodies at t=0 before running simulation.
tools.physics_clear_paint: Remove brushed paint. With no id, strips every stroke in the scene; with an id, that body; with an id and a geomName, that geom. Base colours set by physics_set_color are left alone.
tools.physics_combine:
Merge other bodies into this one and apply a boolean between them. This is how two things you have already built and positioned become one part.

A boolean is a program over ONE body's shapes, so two bodies can never cut each other however they overlap. This brings them together: each merged body's shapes are rewritten into the target's frame — keeping their exact place in the world — marked with the operation, and the bodies they came from are removed, along with anything parented to them.

op 'union' leaves them as ordinary added shapes, which is a compound body needing no boolean at all. 'difference' cuts them out of the target; 'intersection' keeps only the overlap. Both of those turn the boolean on and the result is compiled like any other, so physics_get_object will report csgVolume and the generated source once it has.

Anything can be merged in: a primitive, a lattice part, a sculpt, an imported STL. Build the shape you want to remove, put it where you want it, and subtract it. The target keeps its own id, joints and name.
tools.physics_create_lattice:
Add a lattice body (a shape built by connecting points on a grid) and return its id. This is the only way to make one: a primitive, an imported STL, an OpenSCAD body and a sculpt cannot be converted into one.

Use this rather than sculpting for anything CRISP and DIMENSIONED: a bracket, a housing, a mount, a part that has to be 40 mm across and meet another part squarely.

It starts as a closed box `sizeMm` across (default 40 mm), centred on the body origin. pos is the body's position in world space (default [0, 0, 0.2]); it is dropped in with a free joint, so it falls when the simulation runs. edit:true also opens the lattice tools in the viewport. Only do that when a person is about to carry on by hand: it takes over the viewport and pauses the simulation.

Returns the id and the cage's counts, bounds and size in millimetres. All lattice tools take and return millimetres in the body's own frame, on a 0.1 mm grid.
tools.physics_create_sculpt:
Add a free-form sculptable body and return its id. This is the only way to make one: a primitive, an imported STL and an OpenSCAD body cannot be brushed, and there is no conversion. physics_sculpt refuses anything that is not a sculpt body.

base picks the starting shape (default 'sphere'); see schema.sculpting.bases for the nine and what each is for. Start from the closest base: 'head' is a bust on its shoulders, 'humanoid' a standing mannequin facing +X. pos is the body's position in world space (default [0, 0, 0.3]); the body is dropped in with a free joint, so it falls when the simulation runs.

Returns the id, the base, and the mesh's vertex/face counts, bounds and size in metres. The bases are about 0.24 m across, so a brush radius of 0.04 is roughly a sixth of the body. Start there and go smaller for detail.
tools.physics_cut:
Cut a shape out of a body: a round hole, a rectangular slot, or a spherical dish. Works on ANY body — a primitive, a lattice part, a sculpt, an imported STL — because a cut is an ordinary negative shape added to that body's boolean program.

ON A SCULPT BODY, USE physics_sculpt_cut INSTEAD: a cut made here turns the sculpt into a boolean, and it can no longer be brushed.

THIS IS THE ONLY WAY TO PUT A SHAPE ON A BODY THAT ALREADY EXISTS. A body's geoms are its boolean program, so two separate bodies can never cut each other; physics_combine merges them first if that is what you want.

You say WHERE the cut goes and HOW DEEP, not where the cutter's middle is and how long it is. `at` is a point in the body's own frame in millimetres and `normal` is the outward direction of the surface there (default [0,0,1], straight down onto the top). A line is cast along that normal through `at` to find the material, and `depthMm` is measured from wherever it meets — so 10 mm means 10 mm into the low arm of a bracket as much as into the top of a block. depthMm 0, or omitted, goes right through. The cutter itself is made a little longer than the hole, because a cut ending flush with a surface leaves coincident faces and a boolean of those is not reliably a solid.

`diameterMm` sizes a hole or a dish; `widthMm` and `lengthMm` size a slot, across the surface it enters. A dish is always blind — a ball has no length to run.

The reply gives the point the cut actually landed on, which is not always the point asked for: the line was cast through it to find the surface. NOTE for a lattice body: `at` is the BODY's frame, while physics_get_lattice reports the cage's; the two differ by however far the mesh was recentred on its centre of mass, which physics_get_object reports as latticeOrigin.

WIDTH AND LENGTH ARE IN THE CUT'S OWN FRAME, not the world's. The cutter is made by turning its +Z onto `normal`, so widthMm runs along the surface's local X and lengthMm along its local Y. Cutting straight down (normal [0,0,1]) that is world X and world Y; cutting into a wall facing +Y it is world X and world Z.

TWO CUTS THAT MEET SHOULD OVERLAP, not touch. Negatives that share an exact face leave coincident surfaces in the boolean, and a boolean of those is not reliably a solid. Give neighbouring slots a tenth of a millimetre of overlap and the union comes out clean.

A body that ends up thin and full of through-cuts — a stencil, a fretted plate — may be worth setting to `collision: 'hull'`, which collides it as one filled hull instead of many thin pieces; see the gotcha about hollow shapes.

THE DRAWN SOLID IS NOT WHERE ITS SHAPES SAY IT IS. A compiled boolean is re-origined on its own centre of mass in X and Y, so a plate drawn symmetric about x = 0 with a bore near one edge DRAWS a few millimetres off centre — 4.5 mm, for a 200 mm plate with a 60 mm bore at x = 60. Sizes and the distances between features are exact either way; only the mapping to world space moves.

physics_measure reads the DRAWN scene, so a point measured there has to be converted before it can be cut at: subtract the body's `pos`, then ADD the `csg.originOffsetMm` that physics_get_object and physics_get_scene_summary report. This is the boolean equivalent of `latticeOrigin`, and a lattice body that has also been cut has both.

A TAPPED HOLE: give a hole `threadPitchMm` and it is cut with a right-hand ISO 60° thread of that pitch. `diameterMm` is then the thread's MAJOR diameter — the bolt's name — so an M6 is diameterMm 6, threadPitchMm 1; M3 is 3 × 0.5, M4 is 4 × 0.7, M5 is 5 × 0.8, M8 is 8 × 1.25, M10 is 10 × 1.5. The hole is cut at nominal size: a printed part that must take a real bolt may want a tenth or two of a millimetre on the diameter. Ignored for a slot or a dish. Compiles in well under a second, like any other cut.
tools.physics_get_edges:
List the edges of a body that can be rounded or bevelled, with an id for each. Call this before physics_round_edges when you want particular edges rather than a group.

Edges are found on the body AS MODELLED — holes cut, booleans done, but before any rounding — so ids stay the same while its roundings change. Each is a straight `line` (fromMm/toMm) or a round `circle` rim (centreMm, diameterMm, axis): the edge of a box, the rim of a hole or a boss. Everything is in the body's own frame in millimetres. `groups` says which of top / bottom / vertical it belongs to (by the world's up, whatever way the body is turned), or 'inside' for an inside corner, where rounding ADDS material (`convex` false). `maxRoundMm` / `maxBevelMm` is the largest size that fits that edge on its own: half the narrower face beside it, or half the gap to the next edge on that face. `roundedBy` is the index of the rounding that already has it.

`unroundable` counts edges that are neither straight nor a full circle (a sculpted crease, a helix) — they are left alone. Sculpt bodies are refused with the reason. OpenSCAD and imported parts work; if an OpenSCAD part's source is edited so that a rounded edge is no longer there, that edge's rounding is dropped (physics_get_object shows edgeRoundsLost) rather than cut where the edge used to be.
tools.physics_round_edges:
Round (fillet) or bevel (chamfer) edges of any part except a sculpt — a primitive, a boolean with holes cut in it, a lattice part, an OpenSCAD or imported part. The finishing step that makes a block look made rather than modelled.

`edges` is 'all' (default: every OUTSIDE edge), 'top', 'bottom', 'vertical' (outside edges too), 'inside' (the inside corners, where rounding adds material — a fillet at the foot of a rib makes it stronger), or a list of ids from physics_get_edges. `sizeMm` is the fillet's radius, or for a bevel how far back along each face the cut starts. `mode` 'round' (default) or 'bevel'. A size bigger than fits is refused, with the largest that does. `remove: true` takes the rounding off those edges instead (no size needed).

Each call adds one rounding to the body (listed in the reply's `roundings`); an edge belongs to one rounding at a time, so rounding an edge again at a new size moves it to the new one. The rounding is part of the body's boolean program, so the drawn mesh, the colliders, the mass and every export (STL, CNC, casting) get the rounded shape. A rounded part with no hole collides as its own hull, so a filleted block really does roll off its corners. Where three rounded edges of the same size meet square (a box corner) the corner comes out as a ball's eighth. Where an outside edge runs into an inside corner that is also rounded (the top of a gusset meeting the fillet at its foot) the outside rounding stops at the top of that fillet, leaving its last few millimetres sharp: separate roundings cannot blend into each other there.

FOR PRINTING, BEVEL THE BOTTOM EDGES rather than rounding them: edges 'bottom', mode 'bevel', 0.5 mm — a rounded bottom edge is an overhang.

Resizing a box through its size moves its roundings with it. The reply includes the new volumeMm3.
tools.physics_delete_object: Remove a body from the scene by id, along with everything parented to it. Returns what was deleted and how many children went with it. DESTRUCTIVE and not undoable. Confirm with the user first unless they asked for it.
tools.physics_set_constraint:
Weld one body to another, attach it with a pin, or say what it takes to break the weld off.

`weldTo`/`connectTo` take a body id, null to clear. A weld holds two bodies rigidly wherever they happen to be; a connect pins one point and lets the body swivel about it.

`breakForceN` and `breakTorqueNm` are what the weld survives, in newtons and newton-metres. MuJoCo reports the force it spends holding every weld, so these are real units rather than a made-up scale: a 1 kg body hanging off a weld pulls about 10 N, a few hundred is a sturdy joint, a few tens is decorative. Either limit alone is enough; a weld given only a force limit ignores torque. Pass null to make the weld unbreakable again.

`breakHoldSteps` (default 3) is how many steps in a row the overload must last. A hard contact makes the solver spike for a single step, and without the hold that spike snaps welds that were never really loaded.

BREAKING IS TRANSIENT. It is a simulation event, not an edit: the scene graph still says the part is welded on, so physics_get_scene, exports and share links are unchanged, and physics_reset puts the object back together. Use physics_get_breaks to see what has come apart.
tools.physics_set_impact:
What a body does when it is hit hard: come apart, take a dent, or neither.

Thresholds are in newton-seconds — IMPULSE, i.e. momentum — not force. Contact force in a hard solver is a spike whose height depends on the timestep as much as on the collision, so a force threshold changes meaning when the timestep does. Momentum does not: 0.2 kg arriving at 5 m/s and stopping dead is 1 N*s whatever the solver was doing.

SHATTERING. `shatterImpulseNs` is the blow that breaks the body up; null clears it. The pieces are Voronoi cells of the body's own outline, so they tile it exactly — they weigh what it weighed and start where it was, each carrying the velocity of the part of the body it used to be. `shatterPieces` is 2..24 (default 8), `shatterPattern` is 'radial' (small pieces crowded around the impact, the default) or 'uniform', `shatterSpread` adds outward speed in m/s, and `shatterSeed` fixes which pieces so a scene breaks the same way twice. `shatterDepth` (0 by default, 2 at most) lets the PIECES break again when they land: each shard inherits a threshold scaled to its own share of the body, because a chip held to the whole body's threshold can hardly ever be hit hard enough and reads as armour plating. Pieces of pieces come apart into at most four, and those chips do not collide with EACH OTHER (they still land on and hit everything else), which is what keeps a cascade running in real time. The world holds at most 60 shards at once: a break that would go over cuts fewer pieces, or does not happen. The body must be able to move: something bolted to the scenery cannot be hit hard enough to matter.

DENTING. `dentYieldNs` is the blow that leaves a permanent crater; null clears it. `dentDepthPerNs` is metres of depth per newton-second over the yield, `dentRadius` the crater's radius in metres, `dentMaxDepth` a hard cap. A dent is a displacement of vertices, so a PRIMITIVE has nothing to push in — a box is six numbers the solver evaluates, not eight corners. Setting a yield on one CONVERTS it to the mesh it already looked like, and the reply says so with `convertedToMesh`. Name the surface with `geomName` if the body has several. A plane cannot be dented at all; it is infinite in the solver. A plate given a yield is unmarked by anything under it and cratered by anything over, which is the point: the same plate, two blows, two outcomes.

`pierceImpulseNs` is a second, higher limit past which the surface is HOLED rather than dented — the material under the striker is removed. Keep it well clear of the yield, or there is no range in which the thing behaves like a sheet. The crater's width and shape come from the STRIKER (a flat-ended slug leaves a flat-bottomed pit its own width, a ball a spherical cap) and grow wider as well as deeper with the blow, so the depth rate should be set so that typical impulses land well under dentMaxDepth — a rate that reaches the cap just past the yield makes every blow leave an identical mark and mass stop mattering.

`deformCollision` makes the damage REAL to the solver instead of only visible: things fall through the holes, and an edge worn away stops holding what it used to. It is off by default because it is genuinely expensive — damage reaches MuJoCo by rebuilding the model, and the surface must also be broken into convex pieces each time, since MuJoCo collides a mesh as its convex hull and a hull fills every crater and every hole straight back in. Expect a hitch per blow. Without it:

DENTS AND HOLES ARE COSMETIC. The contact solver keeps using the undented shape, because feeding a deformed mesh back to it means rebuilding the model and that cannot happen at the rate blows arrive.

All of it is TRANSIENT, like a broken weld: the scene graph still holds the whole body, so physics_get_scene, exports and share links are unchanged, and physics_reset makes it whole and unmarked again. physics_get_breaks reports what has actually come apart or been dented.
tools.physics_set_crumple:
A crumple zone: a joint that is rigid until it is overloaded, and then folds and STAYS folded.

Set on a JOINT, because that is what folds — name it with `jointName`, or the body's first hinge or slider is used. A free or ball joint has no single axis to fold about and is refused.

`crumpleTorqueNm` is the torque past which it gives, in newton-metres; null clears it. `crumpleRangeDeg` is how far it may fold afterwards, in degrees, as [min, max]. `crumpleDampingAfter` is the damping written into the joint at the moment it gives — high, normally, so it settles into its new shape rather than swinging into it; without it a released joint reads as a hinge coming undone rather than as metal taking a set.

It costs almost nothing because it is not a new mechanism: the joint is held still by an ordinary weld equality, and giving way is the same release that shears a handle off a mug.

ONE THING TO WATCH: a joint only folds if something is still loading it after it gives. A post standing straight up gives gravity no lever, so once its base yields it simply goes on standing there. A cantilever — an arm held out sideways, already carrying its own weight — folds the moment its root lets go.

TRANSIENT, like every other kind of damage here: the scene graph is untouched and physics_reset straightens it. physics_get_breaks reports it as a key of the form 'crumple:<jointName>'.
tools.physics_get_breaks:
What has sheared off during this run. Returns `broken` (stable keys of the form 'weld:<nodeId>-><targetId>') and `last`, the most recent break with the time and the load it was carrying when it went; `shattered`, the bodies currently in pieces and how many pieces each is in, with `lastShatter`; and `dented`, each marked surface with how many blows it has taken and the deepest in millimetres.

Breakage never reaches the scene graph, so this is the only way to observe it. An empty list means nothing has broken, not that nothing can.
tools.physics_restore_break: Put a broken weld back. With `key`, restores that one joint where the body is now, without disturbing the rest of the run. With no key, resets the whole simulation, which restores everything.
tools.physics_delete_preset: Delete a custom user physics preset by name.
tools.physics_export_cast:
Produce a green-sand casting pattern for the whole scene and report what the pour needs: part volume, cast weight in the chosen metal, the pattern grown by that metal's shrink, the parting height, the gating sizes, and the share of the part that will not draw from the sand.

metal is one of aluminium, brass, bronze, silver. partingFromBaseMm is a height in millimetres from the base of the part, or 'auto' to let it choose. On a part that is symmetric about its own mid-height, parting at the base makes the entire lower half re-entrant, so 'auto' is worth taking.

Pass out_dir to have the pattern STL written there. Without it you get the numbers and the file sizes only: the mesh itself is never returned into the conversation.
tools.physics_export_machining:
Produce a three-axis CNC program for the whole scene and report what the job needs: the stock it wants, the part size and volume, how much of the part no setup can reach, how many holding tabs were placed, the cut distance and the estimated time, plus one G-code program per setup.

sides is 1 or 2. stockThicknessMm 0 takes the part's own height. toolDiaMm sets both the roughing and the finishing cutter. material drives the feeds and speeds: aluminium, hardwood, softwood, plywood, acrylic, foam.

Pass out_dir to have the .nc files written there. Without it you get the numbers and the file sizes only.

It always surfaces the whole part before it profiles it. For something flat that only needs its outline cut — a stencil, a gasket — that is most of the quoted time and none of the useful work.
tools.physics_get_camera: Return the 3D viewport camera's current position and look-at target, both in MuJoCo world-space [x,y,z] (same convention as every other pos field). Reflects the LIVE view, including manual orbiting/panning a human has done in the browser since the last physics_set_camera call or preset change. Call this before a screenshot if you're not sure what's currently framed, or after asking the user to orbit to a specific view themselves. Returns position and target in MuJoCo world space, plus which preset is active.
tools.physics_get_history:
Return the simulation telemetry history, sampled every 10 physics steps (up to 5000 frames held). Reply: { total, returned, stride, frames }, where each frame has time, bodies: { name: { pos, vel, angvel, xfrc_applied } }, joints: { name: { pos, vel, qfrc_applied } }, contacts and aeroDiagnostics.

BY DEFAULT YOU GET AT MOST 200 FRAMES spread evenly across the whole history (stride raised to fit; the newest frame is always included). A full buffer is ~14 MB, so narrow it rather than lifting the cap:
- since_time: only frames at or after this sim time (s).
- last: only the newest N recorded frames.
- stride: keep every kth frame (counted back from the newest).
- max_frames: cap on frames returned (default 200; 0 = no cap, the whole window).
- bodies: only these body ids in each frame's bodies.
- include: which sections to return, any of ['bodies','joints','contacts','aero'] (default all).

Filters apply in that order: since_time, then last, then stride/max_frames. Use physics_get_telemetry for just the latest frame.
tools.physics_get_lattice:
Read a lattice body back: every face, as the corners it is made of, in millimetres in the body's own frame.

Faces come back as coordinates rather than as indices into a vertex list, so a face from this reply can be handed straight to physics_lattice_extrude or physics_lattice_delete_faces. Each face also reports which way it faces ('+z', '-x', ...), which tells an outward face from one drawn from the wrong side.

Also returns the counts, the bounds and size in millimetres, and `watertight`. Call it before every edit that names an existing face: a corner that is 0.05 mm out is not that corner, and the edit will be refused.
tools.physics_get_note_cards: Return the current array of note card overlays. Each card has { id, markdown, minimized, x, y }.
tools.physics_get_object:
Return a single object by ID from the physics scene graph with large mesh arrays stripped.

EVERY MESH GEOM IS CHECKED AND THE RESULT IS IN THE REPLY. Alongside vertCount, faceCount and bbox, a mesh carries `watertight`, and when it is not: `boundaryEdges` (edges used by one triangle instead of two), `nonManifoldEdges`, `degenerateTriangles` and `windingInverted`. A mesh that is not watertight draws perfectly and cannot be printed, cast or machined, so read it before you rely on the shape — this is the same guard physics_get_lattice and physics_get_sculpt have always given you, extended to meshes built by hand or imported.
tools.physics_get_objects: Return all objects in the physics scene graph with large mesh arrays stripped (useful to get SCAD and scripts without massive payload).
tools.physics_get_scene: Return the full scene graph (bodies, joints, geoms, scripts), including raw mesh vertex/face arrays. Can be a very large payload for scad/mesh-heavy scenes. Prefer physics_get_scene_summary unless you actually need the raw arrays.
tools.physics_get_scene_summary:
Return a lightweight scene summary: per-node id/name/pos/quat/euler/joints, and per-geom type/size, or for mesh geoms vertCount/faceCount/bbox instead of the raw vertices/faces arrays. Use this for routine checks (did it compile, roughly what size/shape is it) instead of physics_get_scene.

EVERY MESH GEOM IS CHECKED AND THE RESULT IS IN THE REPLY. Alongside vertCount, faceCount and bbox, a mesh carries `watertight`, and when it is not: `boundaryEdges` (edges used by one triangle instead of two), `nonManifoldEdges`, `degenerateTriangles` and `windingInverted`. A mesh that is not watertight draws perfectly and cannot be printed, cast or machined, so read it before you rely on the shape — this is the same guard physics_get_lattice and physics_get_sculpt have always given you, extended to meshes built by hand or imported.
tools.physics_get_schema: Return this app's full reference doc: geom/joint/node field schema, coordinateSystem (including camera pose), openScadNotes, tips, the gotchas list (25 known failure modes: silent compile errors, text() font issues, script api. prefix, contype/conaffinity collision pitfalls, etc.) and workflow/overview/examples if present. Call this first when building scenes.
tools.physics_get_screenshot: Capture the current rendered frame of the Physics Sim's 3D viewport as a PNG image, exactly as a user would see it (camera angle, colors, lighting). Use this to visually verify a scene's layout, spacing, or shape instead of only inspecting the scene graph numerically. See physics_set_camera to frame a specific view first, and physics_get_camera to check what's currently framed. The frame is rendered on request, so a paused simulation or an idle viewport still gives the scene as it is now.
tools.physics_get_sculpt: Return a sculpt body's base, whether it has been edited, and its mesh statistics: vertex and face counts, bounds and size in metres, and watertightness. Cheap. Call it between strokes to see the shape growing rather than pulling the whole scene graph, which carries every vertex.
tools.physics_get_state: Return full Physics Sim state: sceneGraph, isPlaying, isLoaded, gravity, wind, density, lastCompileError (string | null: the most recent MJCF/MuJoCo compile failure message, or null if the last compile succeeded).
tools.physics_get_telemetry: Return only the latest single frame of simulation telemetry (contains time, bodies: { name: { pos, vel, angvel, xfrc_applied } }, joints: { name: { pos, vel, qfrc_applied } }, contacts, and aeroDiagnostics). Lightweight alternative to physics_get_history.
tools.physics_import_stl: Import a binary or ASCII STL file into the 3D physics simulation. Parses sub-components to infer array spacing and customizer UI parameters (`importMode='scad_parametric'`), raw OpenSCAD polyhedron (`'scad_raw'`), raw 3D mesh (`'mesh'`), or primitive shape approximation (`'primitive'`).
tools.physics_lattice_bevel:
Cut the corners off a face, turning an n-gon into a 2n-gon. `amountMm` is how far back along each edge the cut goes.

Use it to make a round face: smoothing a four-cornered cage gives a rounded square, not a circle. Bevel a square into an octagon and smooth that; extrude the octagon first for a cylinder. Bevel again for sixteen corners if the part is big enough to show it. For most round faces physics_lattice_circle is simpler.

Only for a face whose corners belong to no other face, such as a lone plate before it is extruded. Its edges must run along an axis or at 45 degrees, and the cut must be under half of every edge.
tools.physics_lattice_bevel_edges:
Chamfer or round EDGES OF THE SOLID, stitching the faces back on either side. `edges` is a list of edges, each a pair of corners [[x,y,z],[x,y,z]] in millimetres, or three corners and up for a whole face's border, so "chamfer that rim" is one call. `radiusMm` is how far back the cut goes; `mode` is 'chamfer' (default) or 'fillet'; `loop: true` grows a single edge to its whole ring first; `mirror` cuts the reflection too.

Use this for edges of a solid, not physics_lattice_bevel. That one cuts the corners off a single FACE whose corners belong to nothing else. This one pulls BOTH faces back from the edge and stitches the gap.

Chamfer and fillet are the same cut and differ only under smoothing: a chamfer's strip is held sharp so it stays a flat chamfer; a fillet's is left soft so physics_lattice_smooth rounds it to an arc of about the radius you asked for. A fillet with smoothing at 0 looks like a chamfer.

Pass every edge you want cut in ONE call. A bevel has to see its neighbours to get the corner where two of them meet right, and calling it once per edge cuts the second from a shape the first already moved. Each edge needs exactly two faces on it, must run along an axis or at 45 degrees, and the cut must leave room on the edges either side (half of each where both ends are being cut). A radius that will not fit is refused and changes nothing.
tools.physics_lattice_bridge:
Join two faces with a band of quads, opening both. Both faces are named by their corners in millimetres, and both are consumed: they become the openings of what is now a tube.

On faces of two SEPARATE shapes it makes them one: a neck, a handle, a strut. On two faces of the SAME shape it bores a tunnel through it. With physics_lattice_inset first, this is how a hole through a part is made.

The faces must have the same number of corners and share none of them. Two whole opposite walls of a box share edges through the walls between them, so they are refused: inset each of them first and join the smaller faces.

Corners are paired by the rotation that puts them closest overall, so the band has no twist, and the result is wound consistently whether it joined two shapes or tunnelled through one.
tools.physics_lattice_circle:
Place a circle, or any regular polygon, as one face. `centre` is [x,y,z] in millimetres, `diameterMm` the diameter, `axis` the plane it lies in ('x'/'y'/'z', the plane's normal, default 'z'), `sides` 0 for a circle or 3/4/6/8… for a regular polygon, `mirror` to place the reflection too. Returns `corners` in millimetres. Pass those straight to physics_lattice_extrude for a cylinder, or physics_lattice_inset for a rim.

At the 0.1 mm grid a polygon rounded to it is within 0.05 mm of the true arc. With `sides: 0` the corner count is worked out from the radius against that budget, so a 2 mm hole stays light and a 60 mm disc is smooth, capped at 64.

What lands is an ORDINARY FACE. Extrude it, bridge two of them for a taper, dimension it, mirror it. Prefer this to drawing an octagon by hand with physics_lattice_faces or bevelling a square twice.
tools.physics_lattice_delete_faces:
Remove faces from a lattice body, named by their corners in millimetres, in any order (a face found reversed counts as the same face). Corners that no longer take part in any face stop being part of the shape.

Use it to open a solid up before bridging it, or to take off a face that was drawn inside-out (physics_lattice_faces can also re-draw that one the other way round). Reports how many were removed and which could not be found.

DO NOT EMPTY THE CAGE. Delete every face and the body has no vertices left, MuJoCo refuses the whole scene with 'at least 4 vertices required', and the body is dropped — while these tools go on reporting ok, because the cage edit itself succeeded. Clearing the starter box to revolve or draw something else is the usual way to hit it. Add the new geometry FIRST and delete the box afterwards; the body is then never empty for a moment.
tools.physics_lattice_dimension:
Set the size or the position of part of a lattice shape by saying the number, rather than by pushing it there. `corners` is the corners to measure, as [x, y, z] points in millimetres — a face's four, an edge's two, or any handful — exactly as physics_get_lattice reports them.

mode 'size' scales them about their own middle on that axis, so both ends move and the rest of the part stays where it is. mode 'position' moves them, measured at the middle of the selection — which for a face is the plane it lies in, so "put this face at 20" is one call.

This is how a part gets to be 40 mm across because the thing it bolts to is. Arriving at that by extruding 7 mm and then 3 mm more is arithmetic nobody should be doing in their head.

Every corner named must be a corner of this shape: a dimension applied to three of the four you meant does not fail, it quietly pulls the part out of square, so a name that matches nothing is refused. Values land on the grid like any other placement — ask for 6.35 on a 0.1 mm grid and the reply reads back 6.4. `changed: false` means the request meant nothing: a size on an axis the selection is flat along, or a number it is already at.
tools.physics_lattice_extrude:
Push one face of a lattice body out along its own axis, walling in the gap it leaves. A box becomes an L, a plate becomes a boss, in one call.

`face` is the face's corners in millimetres, in any order; take them from physics_get_lattice. distanceMm is rounded to whole grid steps and may be negative to push the face in. axis ('x', 'y' or 'z') overrides the direction; by default a face travels along whichever axis it faces.

The face itself is consumed: what was the outside becomes the new cap, and the reply gives the cap's corners so the next extrusion can be chained straight onto it. mirror extrudes the reflected face by the same amount.

A single quad extruded is still an open shell: the side it was pushed off is a hole. Cap it with physics_lattice_faces, wound the other way, or start from the box physics_create_lattice gives you, which is already closed.
tools.physics_lattice_faces:
Draw faces on a lattice body. `faces` is a list of faces, each a list of THREE OR MORE corners [x, y, z] in MILLIMETRES in the body's own frame. Use quads wherever possible: Catmull-Clark smoothing puts a dimple at every triangle corner — but an outline that is genuinely a polygon should be sent as one face rather than cut into quads, because a profile split into pieces extrudes into pieces with walls between them. A T is eight corners; an L is six.

Corners do not have to exist yet; a corner that lands where one already is reuses it, which joins the new face to the shape. Points are snapped to the 0.1 mm grid and `snappedBy` reports the largest correction made. A snap of half a step is rounding; a snap of five is a mistake in the numbers.

WINDING DECIDES WHICH WAY A FACE POINTS: corners counter-clockwise seen from outside the solid. A face wound the other way is invisible in the viewport and a hole in the exported file. Check the `normal` physics_get_lattice reports rather than assuming.

mirror ('x', 'y' or 'z') also adds each face's reflection through the body origin, with the winding reversed. Returns what was added, what was skipped and why, and the cage's new counts.
tools.physics_lattice_inset:
Shrink a face inside itself by `amountMm`, leaving a ring of quads around it. `face` is the face's corners in millimetres, in any order; the reply gives the corners of the new smaller face.

This is the start of every hole. Inset each wall first, then physics_lattice_bridge the two smaller faces to bore a tunnel. Inset and then delete the middle for a hole in a plate. Inset and then extrude for a raised panel or a recess.

Only a face lying flat on to an axis can be inset. The inset must also be less than half the face's width.
tools.physics_lattice_orient:
Turn every face of a lattice body to agree with its neighbours and point outwards, and report how many were turned.

A face's winding decides which side of it is solid. A face wound inwards draws wherever backfaces are shown and is lost wherever they are culled, so a part can look finished and export full of holes. Faces drawn by hand take their winding from the order their corners were given.

Every reply from a lattice tool carries `inconsistent`, the number of faces that are inward or at odds with their neighbours. When it is not zero, call this. It is safe to call when it is zero; it does nothing and says so.

Run it before physics_lattice_wall: a wall is offset along the surface's own normals, so on a shape whose normals disagree it is thickened in both directions at once.
tools.physics_lattice_revolve:
Sweep a profile about one of the body's axes, the way a lathe does. `profile` is two or more points [x,y,z] in millimetres in the order they run along the profile, `axis` is the spindle ('x'/'y'/'z', default 'z'), `degrees` is how far round (1 to 360, default 360), `closed: true` joins the last profile point back to the first (a solid ring rather than a shell), `throughMm` moves the axis line off the origin, `segments` overrides how many stops it takes.

Use it for anything turned: a boss, a spigot, a knob, a funnel, a wheel rim. physics_lattice_extrude makes prisms only.

The profile does not have to be drawn first: corners that are not there yet are created, so a whole turned part is one call. HOW FAR EACH POINT SITS FROM THE AXIS IS ITS RADIUS; there is no second number. A point sitting ON the axis becomes the pole, so a cone is a two-point profile: [[0,0,40],[30,0,0]] about 'z' is a 60 mm cone 40 mm tall. Less than 360 leaves both ends open.
tools.physics_lattice_sharpen:
Mark edges of a lattice body sharp, so smoothing rounds everything except them. Pass sharp:false to let them round off again.

Catmull-Clark rounds every edge it is given. Crease the edges that should stay crisp: the rim of a housing, the flat faces of a bracket, the top edge of a knob.

`edges` is a list of edges, each exactly two corners [[x, y, z], [x, y, z]] in millimetres. Take them from the `corners` physics_get_lattice reports; creases already set come back per face as `sharpEdges`. Only an edge some face runs along can be creased; a diagonal across a quad is not an edge.

A corner where three or more sharp edges meet is held in place entirely, so the corner of a box stays square while its faces round. mirror also marks the reflected edge.

loop:true grows each edge into the whole ring it belongs to: the rim of a shell, the top of a cylinder, the seam around a boss. Prefer it to listing a ring edge by edge. A loop runs on through four-way corners and stops where there is no straight on, so on a plain box (every corner three-way) it is just the edge given.

An entry of THREE OR MORE corners is read as a face, and marks that face's whole border. Use that for the rim of a cap: the corners around one are three-way, so no loop runs through them.
tools.physics_lattice_smooth:
Set how many Catmull-Clark passes a lattice body's mesh is built with: 0 (the cage itself, flat faces and hard edges), 1, or 2.

Use this to get curves from a grid: a coarse cage of a few dozen quads, smoothed, rather than a finer grid with thousands of corners.

The CAGE is unchanged and stays what you edit; what changes is the mesh built from it, which is what the physics, the STL and every CAM path see. Quads smooth cleanly and triangles do not, so a shape that will be smoothed should be built out of quads.
tools.physics_lattice_wall:
Give a lattice body a wall thickness in millimetres, turning the surface into a closed shell. Pass 0 to take it off again.

A lattice is a SURFACE. A slicer, a mold and a CAM job all need a closed solid, so a shape that reports watertight:false needs a wall or a cap before export.

The offset runs INWARDS, so a shape drawn as the outside of a part keeps the dimensions it was drawn with. The wall is built after smoothing, so it follows the rounded surface rather than the cage, and the rim where the two surfaces meet is held sharp.

The cage is untouched and goes on reporting itself as open; the mesh built from it is closed. A SHAPE THAT IS ALREADY CLOSED IGNORES THIS, and the box physics_create_lattice hands you is closed. So hollowing that box out means deleting a face first — the one the part opens on, usually the bottom — and then walling the open surface that leaves. Wall a closed box and nothing at all happens.
tools.physics_list_presets: Return available physics scene preset names.
tools.physics_load_preset: Load a physics scene preset. Preset names come from the app's PRESETS registry. Call physics_list_presets for the current list rather than relying on a hardcoded set. Also accepts 'user:<name>' to load a preset the user saved in the app.
tools.physics_machine_arm:
Deliberately CANNOT arm the machine. It exists to give a clear answer rather than leave you guessing why motion is refused.

Arming is a click in the app, by the person standing next to the machine: ARM. That is the one thing in this tool set an agent may not do for itself. If you need to move the machine and it is not armed, ask the user to click it — do not retry, and do not look for another route.

The permission lasts about an hour and covers jogging, zeroing, probing, framing and carving. They can end it at any moment with DISARM in the same banner, which also cancels whatever is running.
tools.physics_machine_cancel: Stop the job and drop the rest of the program. Never gated. The line it reached is kept, so it can still be picked up with physics_machine_resume_from_line. Soft-resets the controller, which leaves it in alarm if it was moving — unlock and re-home before cutting again.
tools.physics_machine_connect:
Open the link to the machine. `transport` is 'usb' or 'wifi'; WiFi also needs `deviceId`.

USB opens a native port-picker that only the person at the keyboard can answer, so it only works if they are sitting there. WiFi has no such prompt and is the transport to prefer — and on a carve it is the better one anyway: through a Tekno Box the device runs the program itself, so a four-hour job survives the laptop being shut.
tools.physics_machine_disarm: Give the permission back before it lapses, and stop anything running. Needs no arming itself. Worth calling when a carve has finished and nothing further is planned.
tools.physics_machine_disconnect: Close the machine link. Does not stop a job — cancel or e-stop first if one is running.
tools.physics_machine_estop:
Emergency stop: soft-reset the controller and stop the spindle, at once. Never gated and never refused.

Reach for this the moment something looks wrong — a cut in the wrong place, a sound that is not right, the user saying stop. Position is lost and the machine needs re-homing and re-zeroing, which is a small price. Do not deliberate about it.
tools.physics_machine_frame_job:
Trace the outline of the stock with nothing cutting. Needs the machine armed.

On a laser the guide beam is lit for this — `guidePower` sets how bright — so the operator can watch exactly where the outline falls on the material. That is the whole point: it answers 'is the stock where the job thinks it is, and is it big enough' in seconds, before anything cuts.

Do this after zeroing and before physics_carve_scene.
tools.physics_machine_goto_origin: Lift to a safe height, then travel to the work origin. `safeZMm` default 5. Needs the machine armed.
tools.physics_machine_home:
Run the homing cycle ($H) against the limit switches. Needs the machine armed. Only works where homing is enabled ($22=1).

Homing establishes machine coordinates; it does not set the work origin and does not make a stale Z datum trustworthy.
tools.physics_machine_jog:
Move the tool by a relative distance: x, y and z in mm, optional feedRate (default 1000). Positive Z is up. At least one axis required. Needs the machine armed.

A GRBL `$J=` jog, so it leaves modal state alone and can be cancelled mid-move. The reply carries the position after the move, read back from the controller rather than assumed.
tools.physics_machine_list_devices: List the Tekno Boxes paired to this account, with whether each is online. Pass one of these ids as physics_machine_connect's deviceId to cut over WiFi. Read-only.
tools.physics_machine_pause:
Feed hold: decelerate and stop without losing position or discarding the planner. Never gated.

The spindle is deliberately left running and the tool is left in the cut — a stationary bit in contact with the work is what burns wood and welds itself into acrylic. Resume with physics_machine_resume.
tools.physics_machine_preview_resume:
What a resume from a given line would do, without doing it. Read-only, never gated.

Returns the preamble it would send and whether the reconstructed state is uncertain. The depth in that preamble is the number worth checking against the workpiece in front of the operator before committing. A program that was streaming when the browser went away is restored from a checkpoint on the next load, so this and resume_from_line now work across a reload, a sleep or a power cut — not only within the session that started the job.
tools.physics_machine_probe_surface:
Probe a grid across the stock and return the heights, for levelling a carve against a bed or workpiece that is not flat. Optional `cols`/`rows` (default 3x3) and `bounds`. Needs the machine armed.

A 0.2mm dish across a 300mm bed is enough to cut through a 0.4mm veneer at one end and not scratch it at the other.
tools.physics_machine_resume: Pick a paused job back up. Needs the machine armed. A tool-change or material pause parks the machine, so resuming drives it back to the cut first; a feed hold only needs releasing.
tools.physics_machine_resume_from_line:
Restart a job that ended badly, part way through. Needs the machine armed. `fromLine` is the program line to pick up at.

This is the tool that turns a dead three-hour carve into twenty lost minutes. Line eleven thousand of a program means nothing on its own — the units, coordinate system, feedrate, spindle speed and depth were all established thousands of lines earlier — so the program is replayed WITHOUT being sent to work out that state, and a short preamble puts the machine back into it: retract, spindle up to speed, move over the point it stopped at, then descend at a feedrate rather than a rapid.

Call physics_machine_preview_resume first and read out the depth it names. And note what this does NOT check: a resume after a snapped cutter is a resume onto a different tool, whose length makes the existing Z datum wrong in the direction of driving into the work. Re-zero Z first.

A job interrupted by the tab closing, the laptop sleeping or the power going off is also resumable: the program and the line it reached are checkpointed to this browser's storage as it streams (and to the account on PhysBox Pro, which is the only option for a program too big for localStorage). The app offers it back on load and on tab focus. That kind of resume is flagged `restored`, and it is the dangerous one: the controller has been through a power cycle, so it is not homed, its tool is unknown, and the work must still be clamped exactly where it was. Home, confirm the work origin and re-zero Z before resuming one.
tools.physics_machine_settings:
The controller's `$$` settings — max rates, accelerations, steps/mm, homing configuration — as read when the link opened. Read-only.

An empty result with a `note` means the controller never answered `$$`, which is NOT the same as a controller with no settings: the figures are unknown, so do not reason about travel limits or feed ceilings from their absence. This app's run-time estimates depend on these, and says when it is falling back to an assumed profile.
tools.physics_machine_status:
Report the machine: whether it is connected, its GRBL state, work and machine coordinates, live feed and spindle, the trim percentages, and how far through a job it is. Read-only and never gated.

`armed` is the field that decides what else you can do. False means every command that moves an axis will be refused until the person at the machine allows it; `armedUntil` is when that permission lapses on its own. Call this before anything else here.
tools.physics_machine_trim:
Trim a running job without stopping it: `feed` and `spindle` take a step of 10, 1, -1 or -10 (percent) or 'reset'; `rapid` takes 100, 50 or 25. Never gated.

What to reach for when a carve is chattering or a cut is scorching, where the alternative is aborting onto material that has been cut into and can no longer be registered.

STEPS, NOT TARGETS: GRBL has no command to set a figure, so 87 is rejected rather than silently ignored. Nudge and check with physics_machine_status.
tools.physics_machine_unlock:
Clear GRBL's alarm lockout ($X). Needs the machine armed.

Routine after a boot lockout. NOT routine after a limit trip or a reset mid-motion: the machine has lost its position and unlocking does not give it back. Home it before cutting.
tools.physics_machine_zero_all: Set X, Y and Z all at once where the tool is standing. Needs the machine armed. The quick setup when the tool is already parked at the corner of the stock at cutting height.
tools.physics_machine_zero_xy: Set the current XY position as the work origin. Needs the machine armed. Jog the tool over the corner of the stock first. Written with `G10 L20`, a real work offset that survives a reset.
tools.physics_machine_zero_z:
Set work Z0. Needs the machine armed. Two ways:
- `touchPlateMm` (default 12): probes down onto a conductive plate of that thickness and puts Z0 the plate's thickness below the contact point. Pass the real figure — a wrong one is a wrong datum, silently.
- `here: true`: records where the tool is standing right now as Z0, with an optional `offsetMm`. This is what to use when the operator has wound the tool down onto the stock by eye, which on a carve is common and perfectly legitimate.

Either way this is what clears the app's `needsZZero` flag. The flag is set the moment a connection opens and again at every tool change, because GRBL keeps the Z offset in EEPROM across sessions, tools and stock — a datum that reads back as valid may belong to a different setup entirely, and nothing in a status report says whether this operator has zeroed this Z since.
tools.physics_measure:
Measure a distance between two points, or the angle at a corner between three. `start` and `end` are points [x,y,z] in METRES in the world frame (the same frame physics_get_objects reports); `corner` turns it into an angle measured at that point; `withinMm` is how far it may snap (default 3); `snap: false` measures exactly the points given.

Each end snaps to the nearest feature: a box's analytic corners, a cylinder's axis and end centres, a mesh vertex, or THE CENTRE OF ANY CIRCLE the neighbouring vertices lie on. That last one makes hole-centre-to-hole-centre measurable on a boolean result, where the document no longer holds the cylinder that cut the hole.

It measures the DRAWN scene, not the document: transforms applied, booleans evaluated, lattice cages smoothed, walled and recentred. Every reply says what each end landed on and how far it had to move (`movedByMm`). If `movedByMm` is large, you aimed at the wrong thing. Distances come back in millimetres and metres, with the per-axis parts in `deltaMm`.
tools.physics_paint: Brush colour onto PART of a geom's surface, as dabs at points on it. Use it for markings: the pips of a die, a stripe down a roller, eyes on a head. Paint adds no geoms, no collisions and no mass. at is [x,y,z] or a list of them, in the GEOM'S OWN frame in metres (the same frame as the geom's pos/size, so a box of size [0.01,0.01,0.01] has its +Z face at z=0.01 and its corners at x,y=±0.01), and every point in one call is one stroke: the five pips of a die face are a single call. radius is the brush radius in metres (default 0.008). rgba is [r,g,b], each 0..1. flow is how much coverage one dab lays down, 0..1 (default 1, full strength; lower values tint, and dabs that overlap build up). Pass erase:true to take paint off instead. Paintable geom types are box, sphere, ellipsoid, cylinder, capsule and mesh; a mesh is painted on the vertices it already has, so a coarse mesh holds only coarse marks. Painted geoms are re-tessellated finely, which is visual only. Errors if no vertex falls within radius of any point; that means the point is not on the surface, usually because it was given in world space instead of the geom's frame.
tools.physics_probe_sculpt:
Find where the surface is. Pass `at`: [x, y, z] or a list of them in the body's own frame, and get back, for each, the nearest point ON the surface, the outward normal there, and how far off the guess was. Nothing is changed.

Use it to get coordinates to sculpt and paint with. The bounding box from physics_get_sculpt locates only the extremities; the belly of a bird, the side of a head, the inside of a hand have to be probed for. Probe a handful of guesses in one call, then sculpt with the points it returns. physics_paint errors if no vertex falls within its radius, so probe before painting too.
tools.physics_reset: Reset the physics simulation to its initial state.
tools.physics_run_headless:
Run the physics simulation headlessly for N ticks. Returns trajectory: [{time, bodies:{name:{pos,vel,angvel,xfrc_applied}}, joints:{name:{pos,vel,qfrc_applied}}, contacts:[{geom1,geom2,dist}], aeroDiagnostics:{name:{relSpeed,alpha,CL,CD,force,torque}}}], warnings:[string]. Does not affect the live view. Use this to verify scene behaviour programmatically (a projectile lands in the right place, a pendulum reaches the right angle, a body comes to rest at the expected position) before calling physics_play for visual presentation. PAYLOAD CONTROL: pass stride=N to keep only every Nth trajectory frame (plus the final frame) and bodies=[names] to include only those bodies per frame. A full per-tick all-body trajectory is ~500KB per 900 ticks and long runs can blow the response window without decimation. For most verification (final position, trajectory shape, lap progress) stride=10 loses nothing that matters.

EVERY REPLY SAYS WHETHER IT FINISHED. `ticksRequested` is what you asked for, `ticksSimulated` is what actually ran, and `truncated` says whether the run stopped early; when it did, `truncationReason` is 'diverged', 'nan' or 'frame-cap' and `truncationDetail` explains it in words.

'diverged' is the one to expect. MuJoCo does not throw when a model goes unstable — it silently resets the state and the clock back to zero and keeps stepping. A run over a scene that blows up therefore used to come back as a full-length trajectory that was really several restarted runs stitched together, with times that climbed, jumped back and climbed again. Now the first tick that fails to advance the clock ends the run and says so. If you see it, the scene is unstable: look for very light bodies, stiff contacts, huge scripted forces, or a composite with too many segments.

Kept frames are exactly `stride` ticks apart, always in ascending time order, with the final tick appended.
tools.physics_save_preset: Save the current active physics scene graph and note cards as a custom user preset.
tools.physics_sculpt:
Brush a sculpt body's surface. `at` is [x, y, z] or a list of them in the BODY'S OWN frame in metres (the same convention as physics_paint). Each point is one dab, and the whole call lands as a single stroke and a single undo step. Points do not need to be exactly on the surface: each is snapped to the nearest point on it, and the normal there sets the brush direction.

A point further from the surface than one brush radius is reported in `missed` rather than applied, and each miss carries `nearest`, the point that would have worked. Feed that back in. This matters on the animal and figure bases, where a coordinate guessed from the bounding box is often off the surface.

brush is one of: draw (push out along the normal; the general-purpose one), inflate (swell the whole area, for mass rather than a feature), smooth (average out lumps and brush marks), flatten (pull the area onto a plane, for a facet or a flat face), pinch (draw the surface together for a ridge, a crease or a sharp edge), grab (take hold and drag; the brush for gross shape, and the only one that needs `delta`, without which it does nothing).

invert reverses the brush: draw carves in, inflate deflates, pinch spreads. symmetry mirrors every dab across a plane through the body's origin: pass 'y' for anything with a left and a right. THE FIGURE BASES ALL FACE +X, so their left and right lie along Y. Mirroring 'x' on a head reflects front to back. The default is 'x'. radius is in metres (default 0.04), strength is 0..1 (default 0.5). dynamicTopology (default true) lets the brush add triangles as it goes, so detail is not limited by the base's resolution; turn it off once the shape is settled and you are only smoothing. detail is the target edge length as a fraction of the radius (default 0.25); smaller is finer and much more expensive.

Returns the new vertex/face counts, whether the mesh is still watertight, how many dabs landed, and the misses. Check the count is growing as you expect: a stroke that reports applied:0 changed nothing at all.

`maxDisplacement` is how far the furthest vertex travelled, in metres, and it is NULL whenever `topologyChanged` is true — which is most strokes, because dynamicTopology is on by default and a brush that adds triangles renumbers the mesh, leaving nothing honest to measure against. Null means not measured, not nothing happened; read `applied`, `moved` and the vertex count for that.
tools.physics_sculpt_cut:
Cut a sculpt body with scissors: a polygon swept straight through the whole body, taken out. A polygon in the middle of the body makes a hole through it; one that runs over the edge cuts that piece off. The body stays a sculpt, so you can go on brushing it, including the new cut faces. Prefer this to physics_cut on a sculpt: physics_cut turns it into a boolean, which ends sculpting.

`polygon` is three or more [x, y, z] points in the BODY'S OWN frame in metres, the same convention as physics_sculpt. It is projected onto a plane and swept along `direction` (default: the polygon's own normal) far enough to go right through the body both ways, so only its outline matters, not its depth. For example, a square of side 0.04 in the XY plane with direction [0, 0, 1] drills a square hole straight down through the top of a base.

mode 'remove' (the default) takes the swept prism out; 'keep' keeps only what lies inside it and takes everything else away. cap (default true) closes the cut with new flat faces so the body stays a solid; cap false leaves the hole open, so the sculpt becomes a shell you can see into. An open shell will not print or machine, and reports watertight false.

A CUT THAT SPLITS THE CLAY MAKES ONE BODY PER PIECE. The largest piece stays on this body; each of the others becomes a new sculpt body at the same pose, listed in `bodies` (this body first), so any of them can be moved, brushed or removed with physics_delete_object on its own. A split cannot be taken back with physics_undo_sculpt (its history for the body is cleared); the editor's undo reverses it.

Returns facesBefore/facesAfter, `pieces`, `bodies` when it split, the usual sculpt summary (of this body) and undoDepth. A cut that does not split the clay is undone with physics_undo_sculpt, which shares its history with physics_sculpt. A cut that would remove all of the clay, or a polygon that encloses nothing, is refused with an error and changes nothing.
tools.physics_set_camera: Point the 3D viewport camera at an explicit pose: position and optional target, both MuJoCo world-space [x,y,z]. Or pass preset='perspective'|'topDown' to reset to a built-in view (this also clears any prior explicit pose). Use this rather than rotating a body to line a face up with a fixed camera: the default 'perspective' preset is a diagonal 3/4 pose ([5,2,5] in Three.js space, looking at the origin), not aligned to any world axis.
tools.physics_set_color: Set a body's base colour. rgba is [r,g,b] or [r,g,b,a], each 0..1; alpha below 1 renders translucent. Omit geomName to colour every geom of the body, which is usually what you want after physics_import_stl: an imported mesh often arrives as several geoms. Colour is decorative only: it never reaches the physics, the MJCF or any exporter. For markings on part of a surface (pips, stripes, a logo, eyes on a face) use physics_paint instead of adding decorative geoms.
tools.physics_set_environment: Update physics environment. gravityZ is negative for downward gravity (e.g. -9.81). windX/windY add lateral fluid drag. density is the density of the surrounding fluid in kg/m3 and it adds DRAG, not buoyancy: MuJoCo's fluid model here pushes back against motion and lifts nothing. A balloon in a scene with density 1.2 still falls. To float something, apply the weight of the fluid it displaces yourself, from that body's script: `api.applyForce([0, 0, rho * volume * 9.81])`. See schema.buoyancy. floorFriction controls ground grip. floorBounce: 0=no bounce (default), 1=maximum bounce. Sets floor dampingRatio to (1-floorBounce), averaged with each contacting geom's own dampingRatio. All fields optional.
tools.physics_set_note_cards:
Replace the note card overlays. Pass noteCards: [{ id, markdown, minimized, x, y }]. One card is the norm; id can be any unique string, minimized false, and x/y in the 20-40 range put it clear of the toolbar. Call this after every physics_build_scene or physics_update_scene, and again whenever an edit changes what the card claims. Pass an empty array to clear all cards.

The markdown should read like a museum label for THIS scene, in this shape:
- `# Title` naming the actual thing built ("Ball Bearing Race"), not its category.
- A sentence or two on what it is and what it does when you press Play.
- `## Dimensions`: the sizes that matter, in metres and kg, as a short list or table: overall extent of the assembly, the size and mass of each significant body, and any gap, radius, or spacing a reader would want the number for. Read them off the geoms you just wrote (geom `size` is a HALF-extent for box and ellipsoid, so a size of [0.1, 0.1, 0.1] is a 0.2 m cube) rather than restating the prompt.
- `## Physics`: the mechanism: which joints, what constrains what, the equation or effect being demonstrated, and any figure worth quoting (period, gear ratio, equilibrium speed).
- `## Try it`: two or three specific things to change, naming the actual body or field to change and what will happen.

Write the numbers you built with; do not round them into vagueness ("about a metre wide") and do not describe the plumbing ("built via MCP", "MuJoCo convex hull"). The built-in presets' cards are the house style: physics_load_preset one and physics_get_note_cards to read it.
tools.physics_set_sculpt_base: Swap a sculpt body's base shape. DESTRUCTIVE: the mesh is replaced outright and any sculpting done on it is gone, so ask the user before calling it on a body they have worked on. Use it to start again, or to correct a base chosen wrongly at the outset.
tools.physics_toggle_play: Toggle play/pause of the physics simulation.
tools.physics_undo_lattice:
Take the last lattice operation back off. The last 8 made through these tools are kept per body, newest first, and every reply carries `undoDepth` so you know how far back you can go.

Separate from the editor's own undo, so it never swallows a person's work. Use it for an extrusion that went the wrong way rather than building over it: an extrusion in the wrong direction leaves side walls inside the solid.
tools.physics_undo_sculpt:
Take the last stroke or cut back off. Use it for a stroke that landed wrong rather than correcting it with more strokes.
