The last 8 strokes and cuts made through physics_sculpt and physics_sculpt_cut are kept, per body, newest first; every stroke's reply carries `undoDepth` so you know how far back you can go. This is separate from the editor's own undo, so it never swallows a person's work.
tools.physics_update_object: Update a single object by ID in the physics scene graph. The updates parameter is a partial object containing any fields from nodeFields (such as scad, pos, euler, script, joints, or geoms) to update and recompile on-the-fly.
tools.physics_update_scene: Replace the full scene graph. sceneGraph is a bare array of SceneNode objects (same convention as physics_build_scene's bodies param). Full control but requires complete valid structure. Waits for any scad bodies to finish compiling and for MJCF to settle before responding. The response is { ok, error?, nodeCount }, so check `ok`/`error` directly rather than polling physics_get_state. Can take several seconds for scenes with multiple scad bodies. After the scene lands, write its note card with physics_set_note_cards; nothing else does. The default card says "Interactive 3D rigid-body physics scene". Replace it as part of building the scene.
tools.physics_validate_scad:
Validate OpenSCAD code and return whether it compiles successfully. On success also returns vertCount, faceCount, and boundingBoxM (the compiled mesh's bounding box in meters) so you can sanity-check real-world size before loading it into a scene. If the compiled bounding box is implausibly large (diagonal >20m), the response includes a `warning` field flagging that you likely forgot to wrap the design in scale([0.001,0.001,0.001]). OpenSCAD designs are typically authored in millimeters, but MuJoCo units are meters, so an un-scaled millimeter design compiles ~1000x too large. On failure returns an error message.

COMPILES ARE FAST. The geometry engine is Manifold, so a plate with twenty-seven holes at $fn=32, or an M8 thread through 20 mm, evaluates in a fifth of a second; $fn=180 on a few dozen features is still a second or two. Nothing is rejected for being dense, and this call waits two minutes for it. Leave $fn at what the machines here can show — 32 is finer than anything they can cut.
tools.use_session: Send every later command for an app to one particular browser tab. port is the app's port (5175 for Mesh) and session_id comes from list_sessions. Selecting a tab that has gone away is refused, and the error lists the ids that do exist.

geomSizes.box: half-extents [hx, hy, hz]. Full dimensions are 2*hx × 2*hy × 2*hz
geomSizes.capsule: [radius, half-height]: a cylinder of half-height hh capped with hemispheres of radius r. Or use fromto to specify endpoints directly. ALWAYS supply both elements (or fromto): a 1-element [radius] does not error, it silently falls back to half-height = radius and collapses the geom into a tiny stub pill at its pos.
geomSizes.ellipsoid: semi-axes [rx, ry, rz]: a sphere stretched independently on each axis
geomSizes.plane: ignored. MuJoCo treats it as an infinite ground plane
geomSizes.mesh: not used; shape defined by vertices+faces. Collides like any other geom regardless of the `dynamic` field: MuJoCo takes its convex hull for collision whether or not dynamic is set. `dynamic` only controls whether the on-screen mesh re-reads the body's position every frame; see geomFields.dynamic.

jointTypes.free: 6-DOF unconstrained; body falls freely under gravity. Use for dropped objects.
jointTypes.hinge: 1-DOF rotation around axis. Specify axis:[x,y,z]. Use for wheels, doors, pendulums.
jointTypes.slide: 1-DOF translation along axis. Specify axis:[x,y,z]. Use for pistons, rails.
jointTypes.ball: 3-DOF rotation (ball-and-socket). Use with stiffness+damping for springs, sway.

geomFields.name: string: unique identifier (required)
geomFields.pos: [x,y,z]: local offset from body origin in MuJoCo Z-up space. NOT world-space: a body at world pos [0,0,0.4] with a box geom of size [0.4,0.4,0.4] spans local z from -0.4 to +0.4 (world 0 to 0.8), not local 0 to 0.8. To place decoration (eyes, labels, etc) on a face, keep the in-face axes within ±half-extent of that axis and set the face-normal axis to ~+half-extent or ~-half-extent. Never use world-height-style values.
geomFields.euler: [roll,pitch,yaw] degrees: local rotation, alternative to quat
geomFields.fromto: [x1,y1,z1, x2,y2,z2]: capsule/cylinder endpoints in local space, overrides size/pos/quat
geomFields.mass: number: override density-based mass for this geom
geomFields.density: number kg/m3: what the geom is made of. MuJoCo weighs a geom by its volume at a default density of 1000 (water), so a hollow or airy shape left at the default comes out absurdly heavy. Ignored when mass is set. Prefer it over mass for anything that may be rescaled, since it keeps weighing the right thing. Oak ~700, pine ~500, concrete ~2400, steel ~7800; a tree crown, a hedge or any other mostly-air volume is single digits.
geomFields.friction: [slide, spin, roll]: contact friction coefficients. slide: tangential sliding (0=icy, 2=rubbery). spin: torsional around contact normal (typical 0.005). roll: rolling resistance (typical 0.0001).
geomFields.contype: integer bitmask: collision group this geom belongs to
geomFields.conaffinity: integer bitmask: which groups this geom collides with
geomFields.solref: [timeconst_s, dampingRatio]: contact spring parameters. timeconst_s: spring time constant in seconds, must be >= 5x timestep (0.005s minimum). Lower = stiffer contact. dampingRatio: 1.0 = critically damped (no bounce), 0.0 = underdamped (max bounce), ~0.2 = lively bouncing. Contact between two geoms averages both dampingRatios: set floor to 0.0 and ball to 0.2 to get 0.1 effective ratio. Default (no solref set): [0.02, 1.0] = stiff, no bounce.
geomFields.solimp: [d0, d1, width, midpoint, power]: contact impedance. d0: min impedance (0.8-0.99), d1: max impedance (0.99-0.9999), width: transition width, midpoint: where transition is centered, power: curve shape. Higher d0/d1 = harder contact, less penetration. Typical bouncy: [0.99, 0.9999, 0.0001, 0.5, 2].
geomFields.vertices: number[]: mesh only: flat [x0,y0,z0,...] in Three.js Y-up space (X=right, Y=up, Z=toward camera)
geomFields.faces: number[]: mesh only: flat triangle indices [i0,j0,k0,...] with outward-facing (CCW) winding
geomFields.dynamic: boolean: a RENDER-path flag, not a physics one. Collision (convex hull) happens for any mesh geom with vertices+faces regardless of this field. With dynamic:true, the on-screen mesh re-reads the body's xpos/xmat every frame, which any body that moves needs. Without it, the mesh renders once from `vertices` baked into world space and never updates, so a jointed body can simulate correctly while looking frozen on screen. Any body with a joint gets dynamic:true defaulted onto its mesh geoms when omitted, so set it explicitly only to be clear about intent.
geomFields.renderVertices: number[]: dynamic mesh only: flat [x0,y0,z0,...] in raw MuJoCo Z-up space. Convert from Y-up: (x,y,z)→(x,-z,y). Do NOT subtract centroid; MuJoCo recenters internally and xpos tracks the result. Auto-derived from `vertices` via that same conversion whenever dynamic is true and renderVertices is not supplied.
geomFields.margin: number: expand contact surface outward by this amount (meters). Useful to prevent sinking.
geomFields.gap: number: dead zone inside margin where no contact force is applied.
geomFields.paint: {res, idx, rgba}: brushed vertex colour laid down by physics_paint, stored sparsely and quantised to bytes. Write it with physics_paint rather than by hand. physics_get_scene returns it verbatim, so it round-trips through physics_update_scene and the app's JSON save/load. Decorative only.
geomFields.dentYieldNs: number — newton-seconds above which this MESH surface takes a permanent crater. Cosmetic: contact keeps using the undented shape. Transient.
geomFields.dentDepthPerNs: number — metres of depth per newton-second over the yield.
geomFields.dentMaxDepth: number — hard cap on how deep one spot can be pushed, in metres.
geomFields.pierceImpulseNs: number — N*s past which the surface is holed clean through instead of dented. Keep it well above dentYieldNs. Cosmetic: contact keeps using the whole surface.
geomFields.deformCollision: boolean — make damage to this surface real to the contact solver rather than only visible. Costs a model rebuild AND a convex decomposition per blow; off by default.

nodeFields.name: string: display name and MuJoCo XML name
nodeFields.pos: [x,y,z]: position relative to parent (or world for root)
nodeFields.euler: [roll,pitch,yaw] degrees: body orientation, alternative to quat
nodeFields.geoms: SceneGeom[]: one or more geoms defining shape
nodeFields.joints: SceneJoint[]: joints to parent (empty = fixed to world)
nodeFields.coupleTargetId: id of body to gear-couple first joints with
nodeFields.weldTargetId: id of body to rigidly weld (closed-loop constraint)
nodeFields.connectTargetId: id of body for ball-socket point constraint
nodeFields.script: JavaScript control script running at 1000 Hz. IMPORTANT: all functions must be called with the 'api.' prefix, e.g. api.getTime(), api.setVelocity([...], 'bodyName'). Bare calls like getTime() will throw ReferenceError. Available: api.isKeyPressed(keyName), api.getPosition(bodyName), api.getVelocity(bodyName), api.getAngularVelocity(bodyName), api.getOrientation(bodyName), api.setPosition(pos, bodyName), api.setVelocity(vel, bodyName), api.setAngularVelocity(angvel, bodyName), api.getMass(bodyName), api.getJointPosition(jointName), api.getJointVelocity(jointName), api.applyForce(forceVec, bodyName), api.applyTorque(torqueVec, bodyName), api.applyJointForce(jointName, forceVal), api.setActuatorControl(actuatorName, ctrlVal), api.getTime(), api.getWind(), api.log(msg). To launch a body with an initial velocity on the first tick: 'if (api.getTime() === 0) { api.setVelocity([vx, vy, vz], "bodyName"); api.setAngularVelocity([wx, wy, wz], "bodyName"); }'
nodeFields.scad: string: raw OpenSCAD source code to procedurally compile into a dynamic mesh geometry
nodeFields.isComposite: boolean: if true, this body is emitted as a MuJoCo <composite> (a chain of auto-generated, auto-jointed segments forming a smooth curve/cable/rope) instead of using this node's own geoms/joints/children directly. Use this instead of chaining many capsule geoms with fromto to approximate a curve. See compositeType/compositeCount/compositeSize/compositeCurve.
nodeFields.compositeType: 'cable'|'grid'|'rope'|'cloth': shape of the composite. 'rope' is remapped to MuJoCo's 'cable' composite type internally; for a smooth 1D curve (rope, cable, mustache, tentacle, vine) use 'cable' or 'rope'. Default 'cable'.
nodeFields.compositeCount: string (NOT an array): space-separated segment counts, e.g. "25 1 1" for a 25-segment 1D cable. More segments = smoother curve but more DOF. Default "15 1 1".
nodeFields.compositeSize: string (NOT a number): total extent of the composite before curving, e.g. "1.5" for a 1.5m cable. Default "1.5". The segments take MuJoCo's DEFAULT DENSITY of 1000 kg/m3, and nothing here overrides it, so the radius is the only thing setting the mass: a 0.9 m cable at radius 0.003 weighs about 26 g, which is four times a helium balloon and will simply hold it down. For anything meant to read as string or thread, radius 0.0004 or so.
nodeFields.compositeCurve: string: MuJoCo composite curve-shape spec (space-separated per-axis codes+params), e.g. "s 0 0" for straight, or a cosine/other MuJoCo composite curve code for a pre-curled shape. Not validated client-side; a malformed string only surfaces as a MuJoCo XML compile error. The chain is laid out along the BODY'S +X before any curve is applied, so a cable meant to hang or stand needs the body turned: euler [0, -90, 0] points it up +Z.
nodeFields.compositePrefix: string: name prefix for the auto-generated segment bodies (default `${name}_`). The last segment's auto-generated name is `${compositePrefix}B_last`, needed if you want to weldLastToId it to something.
nodeFields.weldLastToId: string: id of another body to rigidly weld the composite's LAST segment to (e.g. anchoring both ends of a rope/cable). Only used when isComposite is true. Compare to the general weldTargetId, which welds this node's own body, not a composite's generated last segment.
nodeFields.isCurve: boolean: RIGID curved track. A Catmull-Rom spline through curvePoints is decomposed into many small convex box geoms, so collision follows the real (even concave) curve and balls roll along it. Omit geoms and joints: geoms are auto-generated and the body defaults to static (welded to world). Contrast with isComposite, which makes a floppy rope/cable.
nodeFields.curvePoints: number[][]: body-local Z-up control points, e.g. [[-1.6,0,1.4],[-0.55,0,0.45],[0.45,0,0.12],[1.6,0,0.7]]. The spline IS the rolling surface (segment boxes sit half a thickness below it).
nodeFields.curveSegments: number: how many box segments approximate the spline (default 28; more = smoother)
nodeFields.curveClosed: boolean: wrap the spline into a seamless closed loop (oval/circuit tracks). Default false.
nodeFields.curveBank: number: bank (roll) angle in degrees about the travel direction; positive raises the left-of-travel edge. For a counter-clockwise loop use a NEGATIVE bank to raise the outside edge (the oval_track preset uses -18).
nodeFields.isSculpt: boolean: a free-form sculpted body. Its mesh is not derived from parameters; the sculpt tools own it. Set by physics_create_sculpt; do not set it by hand on an ordinary body.
nodeFields.sculptBase: string: which base shape it was started from. See schema.sculpting.bases.
nodeFields.sculptVersion: number: bumped whenever the mesh is replaced wholesale, so the viewport reloads it. Managed for you.
nodeFields.sculptEdited: boolean: whether any stroke has been applied since the base was set.
nodeFields.weldBreakForceN: number — newtons of pull this weld survives before it shears off. Omit and it never breaks. Transient: reset puts it back.
nodeFields.weldBreakTorqueNm: number — newton-metres of twist this weld survives. Either limit alone is enough.
nodeFields.weldBreakHoldSteps: number — consecutive overloaded steps required (default 3), guarding against contact-onset solver spikes.
nodeFields.shatterImpulseNs: number — newton-seconds of impulse that breaks this body into pieces. Omit and it never shatters. Transient: reset makes it whole.
nodeFields.shatterPattern: 'uniform' | 'radial' — radial crowds the small pieces around the point of impact (default).
nodeFields.shatterSpread: number — extra outward speed per piece, m/s.
nodeFields.shatterSeed: number — fixes which pieces, so a scene breaks the same way twice.
nodeFields.shatterDepth: number — how many times the PIECES may break again when they land (0 default, 2 max). Later generations split into at most four chips that do not collide with each other, and the world holds at most 60 shards.

jointFields.name: string: unique joint name
jointFields.pos: [x,y,z]: joint anchor point in local body space
jointFields.damping: number: velocity-proportional resistance (for free joints, scales drag force/torque to decay velocity and spin uniformly)
jointFields.stiffness: number: spring constant pulling back to springref
jointFields.limited: boolean: whether range limits are active
jointFields.range: [min,max]: joint limits in degrees (hinge) or meters (slide)
jointFields.crumpleTorqueNm: number — N*m past which this joint stops being rigid and folds, permanently. Omit and it behaves as always.
jointFields.crumpleRangeDeg: [number, number] — how far it may fold once it has given, in degrees.
jointFields.crumpleDampingAfter: number — damping written into the joint the moment it gives, so it settles into its new shape rather than swinging into it.

contactPhysicsTips.howContactParamsAreBlended: When two geoms touch, MuJoCo averages their solref and solimp values. This means the floor's dampingRatio directly dilutes a ball's bounce: ball dampingRatio 0.2 + floor dampingRatio 0.0 = effective 0.1 (bouncy). Ball 0.2 + floor 1.0 = effective 0.6 (dead). The built-in floor uses dampingRatio=0.0 so it does not kill bounce.
contactPhysicsTips.defaultContactParams: Geoms with no solref/solimp use the scene default: solref=[0.02, 1.0] (stiff, no bounce), solimp=[0.99, 0.9999, 0.0001, 0.5, 2]. Only set solref/solimp on geoms where you want non-default behaviour.
contactPhysicsTips.makingBouncyObjects: Set solref=[0.04, 0.2] and solimp=[0.99, 0.9999, 0.0001, 0.5, 2] on the geom. dampingRatio 0.2 gives lively but controlled bounce. The UI Bounciness slider (under Physical Material in the properties panel) sets dampingRatio directly, keeping timeconst at 0.04s.
contactPhysicsTips.stabilityLimit: solref[0] (timeconst) must be at least 5x the simulation timestep (0.001s), so minimum 0.005s. Lower values make the contact spring too stiff for the integrator and cause energy explosion. 0.04s is a safe, stiff-feeling default.
contactPhysicsTips.frictionComponents: friction=[slide, spin, roll]. slide (0-2): tangential friction, 0=icy, 1=normal, 2=rubbery. spin (0-0.05): torsional friction around contact normal. roll (0-0.01): rolling resistance; keeps spheres from rolling forever.

meshNotes.staticMesh: No dynamic field (or dynamic:false). Still collides normally (convex hull, like any mesh geom) and, on a body with no joint, never moves. If the body DOES have a joint, a static-flagged mesh geom simulates and collides correctly while its on-screen render stays frozen at its initial baked position, since it never re-reads xpos/xmat. Reserve dynamic:false for mesh geoms on bodies that never move; a jointed body's mesh geoms default to dynamic:true unless you say otherwise. Vertices in Three.js Y-up world space. Good for scenery, decorative structures, visual shells around primitive collision proxies.
meshNotes.dynamicMesh: dynamic:true (or omitted on a jointed body, where it's defaulted). Render re-syncs from the body's xpos/xmat every frame, so the mesh visually tracks a joint or a drag. Collision (convex hull) happens the same way as a static mesh; dynamic doesn't change that. Vertices in Three.js Y-up for collision, renderVertices in raw MuJoCo Z-up for rendering (auto-derived from vertices if you don't supply it).
meshNotes.renderVerticesRule: renderVertices = Y-up vertices with Y↔Z swapped: (x,y,z)→(x,-z,y). No centroid subtraction. MuJoCo recenters the mesh internally; xpos tracks the body frame correctly.
meshNotes.faceWinding:
Use outward-facing CCW winding: each triangle's (v1-v0)x(v2-v0) must point AWAY from the interior. Wrong winding causes inside-out contact normals and objects sinking through surfaces.

IT ALSO HAS A VISUAL SYMPTOM THAT DOES NOT LOOK LIKE A WINDING BUG. Geoms are drawn single-sided, so a backwards triangle is not drawn at all. A whole surface built backwards therefore reads as a body that is HALF TRANSPARENT — you see through its near face to the inside of its far wall — which sends you looking at rgba alpha and materials instead of at the geometry. If a body looks see-through, call physics_get_scene_summary and read `windingInverted` before anything else. The California relief preset shipped inside out and was read as a transparency bug until someone summed its signed volume.
meshNotes.bodyPos: For a dynamic mesh whose Y-up base is at Y=0, set body_pos=[0,0,0]. The mesh will render with its MuJoCo origin at ground level. Adjust body_pos.z to raise/lower.
goodUseCases: Dynamic convex polyhedra (pyramids, crystals, custom shapes)
meshNotes.closedSurfaces:
A MESH YOU BUILD BY HAND IS NOT CLOSED UNLESS YOU CLOSED IT, and nothing in the viewport will tell you. The renderer draws triangles; it does not care whether they enclose a volume. An export does: a slicer, a mold, a casting pattern and a CAM job all need a solid, and all of them refuse or quietly mangle a surface with holes in it.

The usual way to get this wrong is to assemble a shape out of PIECES — a chain of tubes along a path, a stack of rings, a row of slabs — and emit each piece as its own open-ended shell. Consecutive pieces line up so the seams are hidden inside opaque geometry and the model looks perfect from every angle, while every joint is a pair of open rims. Cap every piece, or skin the whole run in one pass sharing a ring between neighbours.

Three faults are fatal downstream: an open edge (used by one triangle instead of two), inside-out winding, and a zero-area triangle from two coincident vertices. An open edge and a zero-area triangle are invisible on screen. Inside-out winding is not invisible, which is worse: it shows as an apparently TRANSPARENT body, so it gets mistaken for a material problem. Check rather than assume: every edge should appear in exactly two triangles, and the signed volume of a correctly wound closed mesh is POSITIVE — sum (a . (b x c)) / 6 over the triangles and look at the sign. Negative means the whole thing is inside out. Positive does NOT mean every face is right: a mesh with some faces each way can still sum positive, so derive each triangle's order from the outward direction of its face rather than writing indices in ascending order and trusting the total.

Separate pieces that must end up as one object have to OVERLAP, not touch. Two closed shells sharing a face are two objects with a coincident wall; two that interpenetrate are unioned into one solid by anything that processes them. Bury a branch's end inside its parent rather than butting it up.

openScadNotes.automaticCompilation: If a body node specifies a scad property and geoms is omitted, the simulator automatically registers it as a dynamic mesh geom and compiles it to vertices and faces. The resulting dynamic mesh behaves as a physical body with collision detection.
openScadNotes.scalingWarning: MuJoCo units are in meters, whereas standard OpenSCAD designs are in millimeters. You MUST wrap your top-level modules or calls in a scale([0.001, 0.001, 0.001]) block. Failing to do so compiles the mesh 1000x larger, which breaks rendering, zoom bounds, and physics stability. physics_validate_scad will flag this for you: it returns boundingBoxM on every successful compile, plus a `warning` field if the result looks like a forgotten scale().
openScadNotes.fontSupport: text() is unreliable in this openscad-wasm build: the bundled font data may be missing or incomplete, so text() calls can silently compile to an empty or wrong mesh. Don't rely on text() for lettering/labels. Instead, hand-build letterforms as vector line strokes: for each glyph, draw its strokes as a handful of thin capsule/hull-of-circles segments (like a single-stroke plotter font, e.g. 'E' is 3 horizontal strokes + 1 vertical, 'V' is 2 diagonal strokes) rather than a pixel/dot-matrix grid of tiny squares. A stroke-based font reads cleanly at small print scale. Keep a small hand-authored per-glyph stroke table (list of [x1,y1,x2,y2] line segments per character) and extrude each stroke with a capsule or a thin rotated box between its endpoints; reuse it across labels rather than redefining per string.

tips: Compound shapes: add multiple geoms to one body with different pos/quat/euler offsets

GOTCHA: geom pos is body-local, not world-space: for a body at pos [0,0,0.4] with a box half-extent of 0.4, local z=0 is the box's vertical center (world z=0.4) and local z=+0.4 is the TOP FACE (world z=0.8). A common mistake is picking pos values as if they were world heights (e.g. z=0.5, 0.55); those either sit right at the surface or float outside the box entirely. When placing decoration on a face, pick the face-normal coordinate at ~half-extent and keep the other two coordinates well inside ±half-extent (e.g. ±60-80% of it) so the feature reads clearly instead of hugging an edge.
Asymmetric shapes: combine box + sphere + cylinder geoms on a single body
Torus-like shapes: ring of capsule geoms arranged with pos+euler offsets
L/T/cross shapes: multiple box geoms with offset positions on one body
fromto on capsule lets you specify start/end points directly in local space

PREFER over manual capsule-chain curves: for a smooth curved/curled shape (rope, cable, mustache, tentacle, vine), set isComposite:true + compositeType:'cable' + compositeCount/compositeSize/compositeCurve on a single body instead of hand-placing a chain of capsule fromto segments. MuJoCo generates a properly-jointed, smoothly-curving chain from one declarative node. See nodeFields.isComposite and the 'Curved Cable (Composite)' example.
Use rgba to color each geom independently for visual variety
ellipsoid semi-axes let you squash/stretch independently on all 3 axes
Children without joints are rigid offsets, useful for adding detail geometry
Arbitrary mesh: type=mesh with vertices=[x0,y0,z0,...] and faces=[i0,j0,k0,...] (triangles)
CRITICAL: mesh vertex coordinate system: X=right, Y=up (height), Z=toward camera. This is Three.js world space, NOT MuJoCo Z-up. The ground plane is at Y=0.
Mesh vertical post example: vertices centred at (cx, halfHeight, cz) with hy=halfHeight (tall in Y)
Mesh flat plank example: box(cx, 0.3, cz, halfSpan, 0.06, halfWidth): small hy=thickness, large hx=span
Static mesh (no dynamic field): visual-only. Vertices in Three.js Y-up world space. Never moves, never collides. Good for scenery and decorative structures.

Dynamic mesh (dynamic:true, or omitted; a jointed body's mesh geoms default to it): renders synced to the body's live position every frame, which any body that moves needs. renderVertices is auto-derived from vertices if you don't supply it.

HOLLOW AND CONCAVE SHAPES JUST WORK — do not build proxy walls. MuJoCo itself collides a mesh as its CONVEX HULL, so a cup, bowl, open-top box, funnel or housing would be solid to contact and a ball dropped in would rest on an invisible lid at the rim. The app now measures each body's SOLIDITY (true volume over hull volume) and breaks anything below ~0.92 into convex pieces automatically, for every kind of mesh body: imported STL, sculpt, lattice, relief, SCAD, boolean. Build the shape as the shape. The old advice to hand-assemble a floor plus wall primitives is obsolete and gives worse results. Override per body with `collision`: 'hull' forces the old filled-in behaviour, 'decompose' forces the split. physics_get_scene_summary reports collidesAs, solidity and cavityFilled. ONE CONSEQUENCE: a decomposed hollow body is weighed by its true volume rather than its hull's, often a third as much, so set mass or collisionMass if you wanted the heavier figure.

GOTCHA: rgba alpha is NOT rendered as transparency in this app: the renderer's material always uses full opacity regardless of the 4th rgba value, so rgba:[r,g,b,0] does NOT make a geom invisible. It renders as solid opaque black (r=g=b=0), which commonly causes flickering/z-fighting where it overlaps another geom. To hide a primitive collision proxy, do NOT rely on alpha. Either color it to match the geom it's layered under (e.g. same rgba as a decorative mesh sitting on top of it) or set contype:0/conaffinity:0 on whichever geom you don't want colliding and accept both are visible.

GOTCHA: how heavy a mesh geom is depends on whether it is closed. A watertight, outward-wound mesh is weighed by the volume it actually encloses. Anything else falls back to MuJoCo's default, which is the mass and inertia of its CONVEX HULL — and for a shape that mostly encloses air (a tree, a chair, a lattice, an open frame) the hull can be a hundred times the volume, with a centre of mass out in space between the parts. A mesh body that is immovably heavy or tips like a top-heavy dome is this: check watertight in physics_get_scene_summary, then set density for what it is made of.

Giving a jointless body its first joint (physics_update_object with joints, or the properties panel) turns collision back on for its geoms IF nothing in the body collided. Scenery is routinely authored contype:0/conaffinity:0, which is correct while it is welded in place and leaves it able only to fall through the floor once it can move. A body that already has one colliding geom is left exactly as it is, and so is anything that ships jointed and ghosted — gear teeth, rotor blades, cradle rods.
Dynamic mesh renderVertices: just swap Y↔Z on each Y-up vertex: (x,y,z)→(x,-z,y). Do NOT subtract centroid. MuJoCo recenters internally.
Dynamic mesh face winding: use outward-facing CCW winding. Wrong winding causes inside-out contacts and objects sinking through surfaces.
Dynamic mesh body pos: set body_pos=[0,0,0] to place mesh where its Y-up base sits. Adjust body_pos.z to raise/lower.
OpenSCAD shapes: set scad="cube([0.5,0.5,0.5]);" on a body node. If geoms is omitted, it automatically creates a dynamic mesh geom and compiles the SCAD code to vertices/faces.
Working example: mesh_collision preset (pyramid + ramp with full collision).
Bouncy objects: set solref=[0.04, 0.2] and solimp=[0.99, 0.9999, 0.0001, 0.5, 2]. dampingRatio 0.2 = lively bounce. The floor has dampingRatio=0.0 so ball+floor averages to 0.1 (still bouncy).
Contact blending: two geoms in contact average their solref/solimp. When tuning, note that a non-bouncy floor (dampingRatio=1.0) will halve any ball's effective bounce.

RIGID curved ramps/tracks: set isCurve:true + curvePoints on a body. Do NOT hand-chain capsules or use a single concave mesh (MuJoCo would collide via its solid convex hull). Editable in-app via the Curve tile: width/thickness/smoothness sliders and a control-point editor.

sculpting.whatItIs: Free-form modelling: the shape is whatever you pushed it into, rather than something described by parameters. Use sculpting when the thing wanted is organic or particular: a face, an animal, a worn tool, a hand.
sculpting.howToWork: physics_create_sculpt from the closest base, then physics_probe_sculpt to find real coordinates on it, then physics_sculpt in passes: gross shape with 'grab' at a large radius, features with 'draw' and 'pinch' at a smaller one, then 'smooth' over the brush marks. Holes through the clay and pieces cut off are physics_sculpt_cut, which keeps the body sculptable. Read the shape back with physics_get_sculpt, look at it with physics_get_screenshot, and physics_undo_sculpt anything that landed wrong rather than patching over it.
sculpting.coordinates: Points are in the body's own frame in metres, Z-up, exactly as for physics_paint. The bases are built around the origin and are about 0.24 m across, so [0, 0, 0.12] is near the top of one and [0.12, 0, 0] near its +X side.

bases.sphere: A ball of clay. The start when no other base is close.
bases.cube: Flat faces and hard edges to cut into. Good for anything built rather than grown.
bases.cylinder: A turned blank: a column, a vessel, a limb. Keeps its axis while you work round it.
bases.humanoid: A standing mannequin, facing +X. Proportion and pose already right; no features.
bases.quadruped: A generic four-legged animal. A session away from a cat, a horse or a bear.
bases.bird: Standing, wings folded. Body, beak and legs placed; feathers are yours.
bases.fish: Streamlined body with fins and a forked tail. Also the start of most sea creatures.
bases.hand: Open palm with the knuckle line already curved.
bases.head: A bust on its shoulders. Skips the hour a portrait spends becoming head-shaped.

brushes.draw: Push the surface out along its normal. The general-purpose brush; inverted, it carves in.
brushes.inflate: Swell the whole area outward. For adding mass rather than a feature.
brushes.smooth: Average out lumps and the marks left by other brushes.
brushes.flatten: Pull the area onto a plane. For a facet, a flat face, a cut-off.
brushes.pinch: Draw the surface together into a ridge: creases, sharp edges, the line of a nose.
brushes.grab: Take hold of the surface and drag it by `delta`. The brush for gross shape, and the only one that does nothing without a delta.
brushes.scissors: Not a brush: physics_sculpt_cut. A polygon swept straight through the body, taken out (a hole, or a piece cut off) or kept (everything else taken out). The cut is closed with new faces unless cap is false. In the app this is the Scissors tool (key 7): a loop drawn on screen, cut along the view.

sculpting.symmetry: physics_sculpt's `symmetry` mirrors every dab across a plane through the body's origin: 'x', 'y' or 'z'. MIRRORING IS OFF UNLESS YOU PASS ONE — omit the argument and each dab lands once, which is what you want for a tree or a rock and not what you want for a face. The bases all face +X, so a figure's left and right lie along Y and symmetry:'y' pairs ears, eyes, arms and fins. Turn it on from the first stroke. Mirroring 'x' on a head reflects front to back, which is almost never what is wanted.
sculpting.colour: A sculpt is coloured like any other body: physics_set_color for the whole thing, physics_paint for markings on part of the surface. A mesh is painted on the vertices it has, so paint a sculpt after the strokes that add detail, not before; refinement changes the vertices underneath it.
sculpting.limits: Only a body made by physics_create_sculpt can be brushed; primitives, imported STLs and OpenSCAD bodies cannot, and there is no conversion. Dynamic topology stops adding vertices at 250,000 and the brush then keeps working at a coarser detail rather than filling memory.
sculpting.makingALimb: Pull it with 'grab' and leave dynamicTopology on, so the surface is refined along the span it drags; without it the vertices the brush caught are stretched over the whole distance and the limb comes out thin and flat. Pull in a few goes, probing the new tip between them, then 'inflate' to thicken and 'smooth' where it meets the body. Two limbs close together need a radius smaller than half the gap between them, or both strokes catch the same vertices.

lattice.whatItIs: Box modelling: points on a regular grid, connected into faces. Use it for parts that have to be exact: a bracket that is 40 mm across, a housing whose walls are 2 mm, a face that meets another squarely.
lattice.coordinates: Millimetres in the body's own frame, snapped to a 0.1 mm grid. Every tool takes and returns them in that form, so a face read back can be fed straight into the next call.
lattice.howToWork: physics_create_lattice for the starting box, then physics_get_lattice to see the six faces and which way each points, then physics_lattice_extrude to push the shape out of it, checking with physics_get_lattice as you go. Place faces by hand with physics_lattice_faces only where an extrusion cannot get you there: a bridge between two parts, a closing cap. Smooth at the end with physics_lattice_smooth, not at the start: a rounded preview makes it harder to see what the cage is doing.
lattice.winding: A face's corners run counter-clockwise seen FROM OUTSIDE the solid. Get it wrong and the face is invisible in the viewport and a hole in the exported file, so read `normal` back from physics_get_lattice rather than trusting the order you typed. The `mirror` argument reverses winding for you. Every reply carries `inconsistent`; when it is not zero, physics_lattice_orient fixes the lot in one call.
lattice.quadsNotTriangles: Use four corners wherever the shape allows. Catmull-Clark smoothing turns every triangle corner into an extraordinary vertex, which shows as a dimple on the smoothed surface.
lattice.watertight: Every reply carries it. An open surface is fine while modelling and fatal to export: a slicer, a mold or a CAM job will refuse it. An extruded single quad is always open (the side it was pushed off is a hole), so either start from the box, which is closed, or cap it explicitly.
lattice.grid: 0.1, 1, 10 and 100 mm, and each is a whole multiple of the finer ones, so a corner placed at a coarse step is exactly on the fine grid. A part can be laid out in tens of millimetres and detailed in tenths without any earlier corner moving.
lattice.limits: Only a body made by physics_create_lattice can be edited this way, and there is no conversion in either direction.
lattice.creases: Smoothing rounds every edge unless it is creased with physics_lattice_sharpen. Build the shape first, smooth it, then crease the edges that should have stayed crisp and smooth again. Creases survive every level of smoothing, and a corner where three or more meet stays put entirely. Use loop:true rather than listing a ring edge by edge.
lattice.wallThickness: Draw the outside of the part and give it a wall with physics_lattice_wall: it offsets the whole surface inwards, reverses the copy and stitches the two together around the border. Check `watertight` on the CAGE to know whether a wall is needed; the mesh that comes out of one is closed regardless of what the cage says.
lattice.roundThings: A square smoothed is a rounded square, not a circle, so roundness has to be built into the cage: physics_lattice_circle places a round face directly, or physics_lattice_bevel a square into an octagon, then physics_lattice_smooth. For a cylinder, place or bevel the face first and extrude it. For a round hole, inset the round face, then bridge or delete the middle.

buoyancy.theShortVersion: Nothing in this simulator floats by itself. Setting environment density gives you drag and nothing else, so a balloon, a boat or a bubble in a scene with density 1.2 sinks exactly as fast as it would in a vacuum, only more slowly.
buoyancy.howToFloat: Apply the weight of the displaced fluid from the body's own script, every tick: `const F = rho * V * 9.81; api.applyForce([0, 0, F]);` where V is the body's volume in cubic metres. For an ellipsoid of semi-axes a, b, c that is (4/3)*PI*a*b*c; for a box of half-extents it is 8*hx*hy*hz.
buoyancy.addedMass: Accelerating a body through a fluid also accelerates the fluid around it. For a bluff shape that added mass is about half the displaced fluid, and for anything lighter than what it displaces it is the larger part of the inertia — leave it out and a balloon launches about twice as briskly as a real one. Carry it in the geom's mass and add its weight to the force, which leaves the net lift alone while making the inertia honest.
buoyancy.whereItActs: Buoyancy acts at the centre of VOLUME and weight at the centre of MASS, and the couple between them is what keeps a balloon knot-down and a boat upright. api.applyForce is a pure force at the centre of mass and generates no torque at all, so a body will drift in whatever attitude it started in unless you also apply r x F yourself from api.getOrientation().
buoyancy.hovering: A constant force makes a body rise until drag balances it and then keep going until it hits something. To make it HOVER, make the force fall off with height the way real air thins: `rho = rho0 * Math.exp(-z / H)` with z from api.getPosition()[2]. Each body then settles where the fluid it displaces weighs what it does, and bodies of different weight stratify at different heights and stay there.

examples.title: BEM Aerodynamic Rotor Script
examples.description: Blade Element Momentum script for a wind-driven rotor hinge. Attach this script to the rotor body. Set windX via physics_set_environment. All blade and hub geoms must have contype:0/conaffinity:0 to prevent contact oscillation. The traditional_windmill preset uses this pattern with 4 blades.
notes: api.getOrientation() returns the 9-element xmat for the script's own body. Column 0 = [R[0],R[3],R[6]] = rotor X-axis in world (the hinge axis direction).
Project wind onto the rotor axis: Vw = windX*R[0] + windY*R[3]. This is the effective axial wind speed.
BEM integrates lift/drag over N radial segments. Tangential force × radius × numBlades gives total hinge torque.
Apply with api.applyJointForce('rotor_hinge', totalTorque). Forces reset to zero each tick before scripts run.
With windX=5, R_blade=0.9, 4 blades, pitch=18°: rotor reaches ~-1.9 rad/s at t=0.5s.

examples.title: Curved Cable (Composite): smooth curve without manual capsule chains
examples.description: A single declarative body that MuJoCo expands into a smoothly-curving chain of auto-jointed segments, the built-in alternative to manually placing many capsule geoms with fromto to fake a curve. Good for rope, cable, mustache curls, tentacles, vines.
notes: isComposite:true switches this body to composite mode; its own geoms/joints are only used as a template (first geom's type/size/rgba, first joint's damping/stiffness), not emitted individually.
compositeCount is a STRING like "25 1 1" (25 segments along the 1D chain), not an array.
compositeSize is a STRING like "1.5" (total extent in meters before curving), not a number.
compositeCurve is a MuJoCo composite curve-shape spec string, e.g. "s 0 0" for straight; pass whatever MuJoCo's <composite curve="..."> attribute accepts.
weldLastToId anchors the LAST auto-generated segment to another body, useful for a rope/cable strung between two fixed points.

examples.title: Procedural OpenSCAD Shape Spawning
examples.description: Spawn a procedural OpenSCAD body at height 2.5m using raw SCAD code, automatically compiling it into a dynamic mesh.

examples.title: Curved Track (isCurve): rigid ramp a ball rolls along
examples.description: A static spline track built from auto-generated convex box segments, plus a ball dropped at the top. The ball follows the concave valley and climbs the far side, which is not possible with a single concave mesh (convex hull) or a floppy composite cable.
notes: curveClosed:true joins the spline into a seamless loop; see the oval_track preset (banked oval + circulating marble).
curveBank tilts the surface into turns: banked-equilibrium speed is v^2 = g*r*tan(bank). Negative bank raises the outside edge for counter-clockwise travel.

examples.title: Chamfer the top rim of a lattice box
examples.description: A whole face border in one call: pass the face's four corners as a single 'edge' and every edge of it is cut, with the corners where they meet handled together.

examples.title: Fillet an edge to a real radius
examples.description: The same cut left soft, then one pass of smoothing rounds it to about the radius asked for. Without the smooth call a fillet still looks like a chamfer.

examples.title: A cylinder from a circle
examples.description: Place a round face and push it out. The ring's corner count is worked out from its diameter, and the corners it returns are what names the face to extrude.
examples.code:
ring = physics_lattice_circle(targetId="boss", centre=[0,0,0], diameterMm=16, axis="z")
physics_lattice_extrude(targetId="boss", face=ring["corners"], distanceMm=12)

examples.title: A turned knob, in one call
examples.description: Revolve a profile that was never drawn. Distance from the axis is the radius; the point on the axis becomes the pole, so the top closes itself.

examples.title: How far apart are those two holes?
examples.description: Aim roughly at each hole and let the snap find the real centres. The reply says what it landed on, the diameters it found, and how far each guess had to move.

machining.overview: Mesh can drive the CNC or laser that cuts the scene, not just model it. The tools are the physics_machine_* set plus physics_carve_scene.
machining.permission: Everything that can move an axis is refused until the person at the machine clicks ARM in the app. You cannot do this for yourself — physics_machine_arm exists only to say so. When motion is refused, ask the user to click it. Reading state, trimming a running cut, pausing, cancelling and e-stopping all work without it, always.
order: 2. physics_machine_connect if needed, preferring WiFi: over a Tekno Box the device runs the program itself, so a long carve survives the laptop being shut.
3. Ask the user to clamp the stock and fit the tool.
4. physics_machine_jog over the corner, then physics_machine_zero_xy.
5. physics_machine_zero_z — with a touch plate, or `here: true` if they wound the tool down by eye.
6. physics_machine_frame_job and let them watch the lap.
7. physics_carve_scene. One SIDE at a time.
8. Poll physics_machine_status. At a tool change, say which tool and what RPM, then re-zero Z before resuming.
9. After a side finishes, tell them to turn the part over, re-fixture, re-zero, and run the next side.
gotchas: A CARVE IS NOT ONE PROGRAM. A solid is cut from several sides with the part re-fixtured between them. Saying "carving now" and going quiet leaves someone waiting for a machine that finished an hour ago and needs turning over.

needsZZero IS SET ON CONNECT, NOT JUST AT TOOL CHANGES. GRBL keeps the Z offset in EEPROM across sessions, tools and stock, and nothing in a status report says whether this operator has zeroed this Z since. A datum that reads back as perfectly valid may belong to a different setup.

PROGRESS IS A CLOCK, NOT A LINE COUNT. A rapid across the stock is one line and a fraction of a second; a raster pass is one line and several. On a relief the mix changes completely between roughing and finishing, so "62% of the lines" and "62% of the way through" are different numbers. Read elapsed against the estimate.

RESUME BEFORE YOU RESTART. physics_machine_resume_from_line turns a dead three-hour carve into twenty lost minutes. Preview it first and check the depth it names — and re-zero Z if the tool changed, which after a snapped cutter it has.
UNREACHABLE GEOMETRY IS REFUSED FOR A REASON. Material the tool cannot get to comes out as a lump on the finished part. Fix the tool or the number of sides rather than overriding it.
DO NOT DELIBERATE ABOUT AN E-STOP. If the user says stop, or something looks wrong, call physics_machine_estop first and work out what happened afterwards.
